articles.summary: Critical Minerals Crunch by 2035: Lithium, Cobalt, Copper Supply Risks - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Glencore
Katanga, Mutanda mines (DRC)
A report from GEM Mining Consulting warns that by 2035 the energy transition will hit a critical-minerals crunch extending past extraction volumes, with processing constraints and shaky project projections endangering supplies. The consultancy, headquartered in Santiago, Chile, projects that supply will satisfy merely 68% of lithium needs in 2035, versus 74% for cobalt and 75% for copper.
Graphite and rare earths pose a separate challenge. Their projected volumes look more sufficient, yet they face heightened supply-chain dangers since processing capacity is overwhelmingly located in China. GEM observed in its report that a reserve gains strategic value only after it can be financed, permitted, extracted, processed, qualified and delivered via a resilient supply chain.
The study pushes back on a conventional approach to gauging mineral security that sets announced mining capacity against projected demand. GEM contends such figures can considerably inflate the material genuinely accessible to manufacturers, since mines encounter permitting and financing holdups, ramp-up difficulties, metallurgical losses and customer qualification demands.
To capture those risks, GEM devised two gauges: a Volume Scarcity Index tracking the shortfall between supply and primary demand, and a Supply Chain Fragility Index assessing elements such as processing concentration, technological dependence and geographic risk.
Lithium stands out as the most volume-constrained mineral, earning 80 out of 100 on the scarcity index. Cobalt receives 65, while copper gets 62.
The outlook shifts once supply-chain vulnerability enters the picture. Rare-earth magnets score 95 out of 100 on the fragility index and battery-grade graphite scores 89, even though projected supply covers 107% and 96% of their respective demand in 2035. Cobalt scores 78 for fragility, while nickel reaches 66 because processing is concentrated in Indonesia and China. Copper, despite its approaching physical deficit, scores a comparatively modest 36.
This distinction means the largest mine-supply deficit is not automatically the biggest strategic weakness. For lithium, cobalt and copper, GEM views the priority as launching dependable new mine production. For graphite and rare earths, spreading refining and processing beyond dominant producing nations matters more.
Rare earths demonstrate the issue. GEM estimates diversified magnet supply outside China would meet only 15% of global demand, leaving consumers exposed even when aggregate worldwide production seems adequate.
Announced project capacity can also mislead policymakers and investors about future mineral availability, according to GEM. The consultancy estimates that a hypothetical project built to yield 100,000 tonnes annually might in the end deliver only about 60,200 tonnes of dependable, saleable output after accounting for development and operating risks, a drop of nearly 40%.
Losses can pile up across a project's development and production chain. Permitting and financing can stall construction, commissioning can defer output, mines require time to hit nameplate capacity and metallurgical recoveries shrink the volume of usable material produced. Material exiting a processing plant may confront a further obstacle: satisfying the chemical and technical specifications demanded by battery, magnet and other manufacturers.
The results imply governments pursuing secure critical-mineral supplies may need to look past headline resource estimates or planned mine capacity. Processing infrastructure, financing, permitting, technical performance and the capacity to deliver qualified material all decide whether underground resources turn into usable supply.
For miners and investors, GEM contends this alters how projects ought to be valued. A smaller deposit with established processing, infrastructure and customers may hold greater strategic weight than a far larger resource lacking a dependable route to market. The energy transition's mineral contest, put differently, may hinge as much on what occurs after ore leaves the ground as on how much miners can extract.

articles.title: Copper and Nickel Prices Could Double Within a Decade - Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.summary: Copper and Nickel Prices Could Double Within a Decade  Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.full_text:
Copper and nickel prices are projected to roughly double over the next decade as demand from construction, electrification, and clean energy technologies outpaces supply growth, with supply deficits averaging around 10% of demand by 2035.
- Supply-demand gap: Copper and nickel supply expected to grow only 1-1.5% annually, while demand grows about 1.8% yearly, creating significant shortages by 2035.
- Clean energy impact: Clean energy technologies alone could account for approximately 35% of global copper and nickel demand by 2035, driven by electrification and battery manufacturing.
- Refined copper deficit: Coface projects a refined copper deficit of 1.5-6.5 million tons by 2035, representing about 11% of projected demand.
- Trade barriers surge: Global import and export restrictions on minerals have more than tripled to 1,138 by end of 2025, up from 357 a decade earlier.
- China's dominance: China controls approximately 70% of refining capacity for 19 of 20 key minerals, limiting supply alternatives globally.
Prices for copper and nickel could roughly double over the next decade as demand from construction, electrification and clean energy outpaces what mines and refiners can deliver, according to Back to the Future (Cycle) from Coface.
The report projects that aluminum, copper and nickel will face supply deficits averaging around 10% of demand by 2035.
"U.S. tariffs are part of a much larger shift in how metals are traded," says Marcos Carias, North America economist at Coface. "Governments have been restricting metals trade for years, and the U.S. measures add to that pressure at a time when supply is already falling behind demand. For manufacturers in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, that means planning for higher metal costs over the long term instead of waiting for a trade deal to bring prices back down."
Key takeaways:
- Over the next decade, supply is expected to grow just 0.4% a year for aluminum, 1% for copper and 1.5% for nickel. Demand for all three is projected to grow about 1.8% a year, and faster under a net zero scenario.
- Clean energy technologies alone could account for about 35% of global copper and nickel demand by 2035.
- Close to three-quarters of global copper demand now goes to electrification, and the rapid buildout of data centers is adding to it.
- Coface projects a refined copper deficit of 1.5-6.5 million tons by 2035, about 11% of projected demand. Under a net-zero scenario, the gap could reach 17%.
- Under a net-zero scenario, the refined nickel market could face a deficit of roughly 35% of projected demand, driven largely by battery manufacturing.
- A deficit of 5-15 million tons, or about 10% of demand, reflects limits on low-cost electricity and smelting capacity rather than a lack of raw material.
- Both have less exposure to energy transition demand, so price increases are expected to be more moderate.
- Trade barriers have more than tripled. By the end of 2025, 1,138 import and export restrictions on minerals were in force, up from 357 a decade earlier.
- China holds around 70% of refining capacity for 19 of 20 key minerals and produces more than half of the world's steel, aluminum and refined copper.
- Fewer than 1% of exploration projects become working mines, and development timelines of 15-20 years limit how fast output can respond to higher prices.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Drives OPEC+ Oil Production Higher in September - energynews.pro
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia Drives OPEC+ Oil Production Higher in September  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Oil production by the OPEC+ group rose markedly in September, led by Saudi Arabia, according to the monthly report of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) published on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The increase comes despite the war against Iran and the attack on the Saudi East-West pipeline. In the same document, OPEC again lowers its demand forecast for the current year and raises the one for the following year.
A Saudi increase that depends on the source used
Total OPEC+ output remains far below its pre-war level. Saudi Arabia, the largest producer within the group's core, remains well short of its quota, and the quota increases decided over the year have largely remained theoretical. In early October, the alliance's core chose to freeze required production levels for one more month.
The scale of the Saudi rebound varies by data series. According to figures Riyadh reported directly to OPEC, production would have jumped from one month to the next. Secondary sources, the official basis for the organization's aggregate calculations, show a real but more modest increase. In August, the Saudi declaration was below the external estimate; in September, it is above it.
The East-West pipeline at the center of flows
Saudi Arabia had redirected a large share of its exports to the Red Sea through the East-West pipeline, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Drones from Iraq struck the infrastructure in September, and Riyadh closed it as a precaution. Saudi Aramco then shifted its loadings to its Gulf terminals, including Ras Tanura, with ship-to-ship transfers off Oman.
The pipeline was repaired and partially resumed operations toward the end of the month. Saudi crude exports rose sharply over September, but Europe was left without Saudi deliveries for the following month. Separately, Yemen's Houthis claimed further strikes on Aramco facilities at Yanbu, without Saudi confirmation.
An unevenly recovering Gulf
Across the Gulf, the recovery remains uneven. Crude and condensate flows are approaching their pre-war level, while refined product exports remain well behind. Iranian exports have fallen to zero under the US blockade, while OPEC's secondary sources continue to attribute substantial production to Iran.

articles.title: Oil prices diverge as Brent falls below $106, WTI rises; OPEC Basket jumps 4.14% - Gulf News
articles.summary: Oil prices diverge as Brent falls below $106, WTI rises; OPEC Basket jumps 4.14%  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
Oil benchmarks show mixed trends with OPEC Basket leading gains
Global oil benchmarks moved in different directions early Wednesday, with US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rising while Brent and Abu Dhabi's Murban crude declined, according to market quotes at 7:31 a.m. Tokyo time.
WTI crude futures rose 63 cents, or 0.67%, to $94.77 a barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell 96 cents, or 0.9%, to $105.69 a barrel.
Murban crude, a key benchmark for Abu Dhabi oil, dropped $1.67, or 1.49%, to $110.57 a barrel.
The OPEC Basket recorded the strongest percentage gain among the listed benchmarks, rising $4.53, or 4.14%, to $114.03 a barrel.
The divergence suggests a mixed session across crude markets rather than a uniform move in global oil prices. The figures represent a snapshot of market quotes, and differences in benchmark pricing periods and update schedules may affect comparisons.
Oil traders are weighing competing forces: continued risks to Middle East supply routes, the prospect of additional Russian diesel supplies and concerns about global demand.
Reuters reported on October 13 that Brent settled 0.9% lower at $105.69 a barrel, while WTI rose to $94.14. The market was balancing regional security risks against the possibility of additional fuel supplies from Russia.
Shipping costs are another concern. OPEC and non-OPEC producers warned on October 12 that shipping and insurance costs for energy flows had surged to more than one-third of commodity value in some cases, adding to inflationary pressures.
OPEC's October report also showed that combined OPEC+ oil production increased by about 900,000 barrels per day in September, reaching 39.07 million bpd.
Yet higher production does not automatically resolve supply disruptions when shipping routes, insurance and delivery costs remain uncertain.

articles.title: JPMorgan names critical minerals chief for $1.5T push - Mining.com
articles.summary: JPMorgan names critical minerals chief for $1.5T push  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
JPMorganChase (NYSE: JPM) has appointed Andrew Frame to lead critical minerals investment efforts under its $1.5-trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative (SRI), placing him at the centre of a push to strengthen US and allied supply chains for materials essential to manufacturing, energy and defence.
Frame will oversee the bank’s critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, identifying investment opportunities and addressing bottlenecks that threaten access to strategic resources. His mandate forms part of JPMorganChase’s 10-year initiative to facilitate financing and investment in industries considered vital to economic and national security.
“It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing—all of which are essential for our national security,” JPMorganChase chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon said when the initiative was announced.
Frame’s appointment comes as Western governments and companies seek to diversify mineral supplies and reduce their exposure to concentrated overseas production and processing capacity. Securing reliable sources of these materials has become increasingly important for defence systems, electric vehicles, renewable energy infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Priorities
JPMorganChase’s SRI targets four broad sectors: supply chains and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier technologies.
The bank has identified 27 subcategories within those sectors, including critical minerals, nuclear energy, battery storage, semiconductors, robotics and advanced defence components.
Critical minerals, pharmaceutical precursors and robotics fall under the manufacturing category, while defence investments will target autonomous systems, drones, secure communications and aerospace technologies.
Energy financing will include nuclear power, battery storage, distributed energy and electrical grid resilience. The technology portfolio will cover artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, quantum computing and other emerging industries, including semiconductors and nanomaterials.
Since October 2025, the bank has been supporting companies ranging from middle-market businesses to large corporations through lending, financial advisory services and selective direct investments.
The financing commitment involves facilitating and financing transactions for clients, with the separate $10-billion allocation earmarked for potential equity and venture capital investments.
Support expansion
JPMorganChase plans to recruit additional bankers, investment professionals and industry specialists to support the initiative. It will also establish an external advisory council comprising public- and private-sector leaders to help shape its long-term strategy.
The bank’s existing relationships could provide a broad platform for deploying capital. It serves 34,000 mid-sized companies and more than 90% of Fortune 500 businesses, alongside established private equity and venture capital partners.
Its Commercial & Investment Bank has held a leading position in global investment banking for more than 15 years, with experience financing and advising companies in defence, aerospace, healthcare and energy.
The initiative has drawn on research into private companies, rare earth supply chains and emerging technologies. JPMorganChase’s recently established a Center for Geopolitics that will provide analysis of international developments, while its Asset & Wealth Management division will contribute investment expertise.
Beyond financing, the bank intends to advocate for policies that encourage research and development, streamline permitting and procurement, and reduce regulatory barriers. It also plans to work with business and community partners to strengthen workforce training in industries facing shortages of skilled labour.
Further implementation will depend partly on the ability of companies to advance projects through permitting, secure qualified workers and establish commercially viable operations. The initiative sets out financing ambitions rather than guaranteed spending or completed investments.
Frame’s appointment gives the bank a dedicated leader to address those challenges across the minerals value chain.

articles.summary: Mining investment firm Appian appoints dedicated experts to boost critical minerals portfolio  Mining Weekly
articles.full_text:
Atlantic Strategic Minerals' mineral sands operation
As investment adviser Appian Capital Advisory builds out its critical minerals portfolio to serve industrial and defence supply chains, the company has established a base in Washington DC, and appointed Brian Greeley CFO of critical minerals and Christoper Smith and John Meier as senior advisers.
Greeley formerly worked as senior VP and chief banking officer at the US Export-Import Bank, while Smith previously worked as chief government affairs officer at Ford Motor Company. Meier is a retired Rear Admiral of the US Navy.
The appointments bring direct experience across finance, industrial government affairs, public-private financing and defence procurement, which complements Appian's in-house technical team as it advances its existing critical minerals portfolio.
The critical minerals portfolio has a planned development capital pipeline of $2.5-billion over the next five years.
The additions strengthen Appian’s capabilities as it evaluates further critical minerals opportunities, helping ensure new investments are underwritten and structured to meet the specifications and offtake demands of industrial and defence supply chains. In turn, the presence in Washington DC reflects the firm's commitment to deepening its engagement with industrial defence and policy stakeholders.
Appian's portfolio currently spans cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, mineral sands, nickel and rare earths assets, including Atlantic Strategic Minerals' mineral sands operation and the largest minerals separation plant in North America.
Atlantic is working to build domestic rare earths processing capacity in Virginia.
Notably, another investment of Appian is that of Gippsland Critical Minerals, which owns the advanced-stage Fingerboards project in Australia, which Appian says has the potential to provide 7.1% of the world's heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium supply.
"These appointments reflect the growing complexity of sourcing, financing and delivering critical minerals projects at the pace industrial and government customers now require. Greeley, Smith and Meier bring direct experience and strengthen our ability to scale the critical minerals portfolio in step with the partners who rely on its supply," says Appian founder and CEO Michael Scherb.
"Mining is a highly technical industry, and without that expertise, organisations struggle to select and advance assets to reach production. Appian has the largest in-house technical team of any private capital investor in mining and is uniquely positioned to support not only asset selection but operatorship as well," he adds.
“In my experience structuring financing for critical minerals projects, I saw firsthand how aligning private capital with policy goals can accelerate projects to completion and meaningful production. Appian’s in-house technical expertise is a unique differentiator in the industry," comments Greeley.
He concludes that private capital must play a significant role in building global critical mineral supply chains, and Appian is positioned to be at the forefront of this effort.

articles.title: Chinese Mining Expansion Devours Congolese City in Race for Critical Minerals - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: Chinese Mining Expansion Devours Congolese City in Race for Critical Minerals  The China-Global South Project
articles.full_text:
- Industrial mining by Commus and others is swallowing Kolwezi, turning neighborhoods into open pits and eroding urban space.
- Residents such as Chibang Kasump in Musonoi face relocation, pollution, damaged homes, and uncertain or delayed compensation.
- DRC supplies most global cobalt and vast copper; artisanal diggers risk death as China and the U.S. race for minerals.
From his yard, Chibang Kasump sees the comings and goings of the miners who dig for copper and cobalt, day and night, deep below his small, brick home in the southern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The 47-year-old has lived for more than a decade in the Musonoi area of Kolwezi, the country’s mining capital, which sits atop coveted deposits at the center of a global race for critical minerals.
“I bought this house because it was quiet, close to the city center and near the lake,” he told AFP. “I didn’t know there were minerals beneath my feet,” he said. “Now I live with a well in my yard.”
The vast central African nation produces around 70 percent of global cobalt output — key for making electric batteries and in defense technology — and holds some of the world’s richest deposits of copper, a metal in growing demand as countries expand electrical networks to harness renewable energies.
Mining companies and foreign investors have stepped up their expansion efforts, explorations and asset acquisitions. The next few years are expected to bring exponential growth in demand for critical metals that are indispensable to global industry.
China has been investing in the DRC for two decades.
The U.S. signed a strategic partnership deal with the Congolese government in December, hoping to shore up supplies for its high-tech industry. Kasump’s plot lies within the Tondo Mining Company’s concession.
The Congolese firm holds the operating license for the site, which is next to the vast copper and cobalt deposit of the Chinese company Commus.
Ahead of an industrial mining operation being set up, artisanal miners — known as diggers — have moved into the area — right up to Kasump’s yard.
Relocated
The boundary between urban space and mining land is fading in Kolwezi, in the heart of the African copper belt. Open-pit mines are gradually eating away at neighborhoods, while concessions are piling up on top of one another.
In Musonoi, the houses have numbers spray-painted on them. “All the houses are identified for relocation,” Kazadi Roger, a local administrative official, said.
“The mining company is going to provide compensation, but people still don’t know when they’ll be leaving,” he added.
Under Congolese mining law, a land title does not confer any rights over the minerals present in the subsoil. But a mining title also does not cancel out the rights of the occupants of a plot, who must be compensated in the event of expropriation.
Kasump initially refused but said “with the pollution, the explosions linked to the extraction, I ended up saying ‘yes.'”
He does not know how much he will receive or where he will move to, though. Behind him, dump trucks rolled by, nonstop, along the road carved out by the neighboring Chinese industrial mine. The dust settles on the rooftops and rainwater seeps into houses that have cracked as a result of the mining.
Under a white tarpaulin adjoining his house, a yawning chasm appeared in the ground into which a young digger disappeared. A pump hummed softly, sending oxygen to those who had descended into the darkness.
At a depth of around 100 meters (328 feet), some 30 men hacked away at the rock with pickaxes, filling sacks.
Using a rope, a human chain carried the ore — mostly copper — to the surface.
Risking Lives to Dig
“We follow the vein,” one of the diggers said. “When we see the grade is good, we stop.”
The timber lining the walls acts as a support but even the slightest collapse can prove fatal. Some diggers earn around $500 a month, others much less, depending on how much ore they have recovered and its quality. All the artisanal stakeholders interviewed complained that the artisanal mining zones (ZEA), which are provided for by law, were insufficient.
“Everywhere, concessions have already been granted,” Sylvestre Petit-Petit, the artisanal miners’ local representative, grumbled. “The state has not given enough space to the diggers,” he added.
As a result, they work in private concessions, often without authorization. Some break into large industrial mines, risking their lives.
“Over there, they’re shooting at us,” one of them said, adding he had lost “several friends” that way.
The extracted ore is washed, sold to traders who are often Chinese, and then undergoes initial processing before being exported.
“The mines advance; the city retreats,” said Aaron Niumbi, a young resident of another Kolwezi neighborhood.
He, too, faces having to move out due to the expansion plans of China’s Commus.

Rare earth elements have become one of the most strategic corners of the mining world, and Nordique Critical Metals Inc. (TSXV:NQC) NQC (TSXV:NQC) has just secured a key step toward a meaningful position. The Montral-based explorer, formerly known as Consolidated Lithium Metals and a constituent of the TSX Venture Composite Index, received final approval from the TSX Venture Exchange for its acquisition of an option to earn up to a majority interest in the Kwyjibo rare earth project in Qubec. Alongside the approval, it filed an amended preliminary economic assessment report for the project. Together, the developments mark a turning point for a company that has repositioned itself around critical minerals.
Final Exchange Approval
Final approval from the TSX Venture Exchange allows Nordique to proceed with the option agreement it announced earlier. Under the option, the company can earn an interest in Kwyjibo by meeting certain conditions, such as funding work and making payments over time.
From Lithium to Rare Earths
The companys name change from Consolidated Lithium Metals to Nordique Critical Metals reflects a broader focus on critical minerals beyond lithium. Rare earths add exposure to a market closely tied to permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence systems.
The Kwyjibo Project
Kwyjibo is a rare earth project in Qubec that has been studied through a preliminary economic assessment. Such assessments provide an early look at a projects possible economics, including mining methods, processing and costs, though they rely on early-stage information.
The Amended PEA
Filing an amended assessment report updates the technical documentation supporting the project. Technical reports must meet Canadian disclosure standards, giving the market a consistent basis for evaluating the project.
Why Rare Earths Matter
China dominates global rare earth mining and processing, prompting Western governments to support new sources of supply. Projects in stable jurisdictions like Qubec can attract interest from policymakers and manufacturers seeking secure supply chains. For followers of Metal & Mining Stocks, Nordique offers early-stage exposure to that theme.
Qubecs Critical Minerals Strategy
Qubec has promoted itself as a destination for critical mineral development, with access to hydroelectric power, infrastructure and a skilled mining workforce.
How Option Agreements Work
Option agreements allow a company to earn into a project over time rather than paying the full value upfront. Typical conditions include exploration spending, cash or share payments and reaching certain milestones. If conditions are met, the company earns its interest.
Benefits for Juniors
This structure lets smaller companies gain exposure to advanced projects without a large initial outlay, preserving cash for technical work.
Inside a Preliminary Economic Assessment
A preliminary economic assessment is an early-stage study that estimates how a mining project might be developed and operated. It typically outlines possible mining methods, processing routes, capital and operating costs, and a rough view of project economics.
Because these studies often rely on inferred resources and early engineering, they carry more uncertainty than later-stage feasibility studies. Even so, they help companies decide whether a project is worth advancing and where further work is needed.
Why Amendments Happen
Companies sometimes amend technical reports to update information, correct details or meet disclosure requirements. An amended filing provides the most current version of the technical basis for a project.
The Rare Earth Supply Chain
Rare earth projects face challenges beyond mining. The elements must be separated and refined into individual oxides, a complex chemical process that has been concentrated in a few countries. Developing projects in North America often involves partnerships with processors or plans for local processing capacity.
Demand Drivers
Permanent magnets made with neodymium and praseodymium are essential for electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, robotics and defence equipment. Growth in these markets supports long-term interest in rare earth projects.
What It Means for Nordique
For a junior company, securing a path to a significant interest in an advanced project can be transformational. It gives Nordique a flagship asset with existing technical work, rather than starting from early exploration.
Work to satisfy the option conditions and advance Kwyjibo, along with any financing to support that work, will be the next milestones.

articles.title: Brazil rare earth deal proves militaries’ long-held interest in minerals - Dialogue Earth
articles.summary: Brazil rare earth deal proves militaries’ long-held interest in minerals  Dialogue Earth
articles.full_text:
In 1939, the term “critical minerals” entered the legislative lexicon of the US when the country passed its Strategic and Critical Materials Stock Piling Act. They became defined as materials needed to supply military and industrial needs during a national emergency.
As that definition expanded through the 1970s and 1980s and into the 21st century, the origin story was gradually forgotten. Discussions on critical minerals today revolve around the energy transition: wind turbines, electric cars, batteries. However, a recent rare earth minerals deal serves as a reminder that this backstory remains – and may even be becoming more prominent.
In late August, the US Department of War announced a USD 750 million investment to secure supplies from the Serra Verde rare earths mine in Goiás, central-west Brazil.
Serra Verde produces dysprosium, terbium, neodymium and praseodymium, four of the 17 elements known as the rare earth minerals. Roughly half of global rare earth supplies are used to make permanent magnets. These magnets are used in wind turbines and electric vehicles, but also fighter jets, missiles and drones.
The interests of the global energy transition have become uncomfortably entwined with those of the military industrial complex. With the world increasingly insecure and ongoing tensions informing US-China trade relations, that has become all too difficult to ignore.
“Critical minerals were born in wartime,” says Phil Johnstone, a visiting fellow at the University of Sussex in the UK. “[Sustainability goals grew] in a time where it was basically accepted that the world was aiming for peace. The world’s changed and that is not the case anymore. Extraordinary things are happening that we couldn’t have imagined a few years ago.”
Brazil’s rare earths
Commercial production began at Serra Verde’s Pela Ema deposit in 2024, with a view to producing 6,400 tonnes of rare earth oxides a year by the end of 2027. The company claims to be the first “scale” producer of the four main rare earths outside Asia.
The US Department of War announced its investment as part of a wider USD 1.55 billion initiative spearheaded by its “economic defense unit”, saying: “This strategic partnership will establish a secure supply chain for rare earth elements critical for national defense and economic security.”
These are 17 varieties of heavy metal chemical elements distributed throughout Earth’s crust. Worldwide, there are 110 million tonnes of rare earths reserves, the US Geological Survey estimated in 2024.
The rare earths all have similar but unusual chemical and physical properties that make them critical for many modern technologies. For example, gadolinium is used in nuclear power reactors, while scandium finds use in vehicle fuel cells.
Rare earth elements fall under the broader term of critical minerals, which are key ingredients for modern technology. For example, the critical mineral lithium is vital for electric vehicle batteries, while nickel is used in stainless steel.
This interest reflects the security concerns that are increasingly shaping US foreign policy in Latin America and beyond. Over the past two decades, China has built a dominant position in critical minerals processing, representing 91% of the global production of refined rare earth output, and 94% of sintered permanent magnets (crucial components in the motors commonly used in, for example, wind turbines and defence systems).
The dominance of its main geopolitical and economic rival over the supply chain creates a strategic vulnerability for Washington, which relies on Chinese-made magnets and other technologies for its military hardware.
For Latin American countries, this renewed interest from the US in natural resources creates a dilemma: the White House under President Trump has shown itself willing to intervene directly in the region, as seen in Venezuela; on the other hand, China remains a key trading partner for most of the region. Careful balancing acts have become necessary.
The Trump administration has also put particular pressure on states where it deems Chinese investment could represent a “dual use” – the second use being the military. This was a key concern in Panama, where a court ruled that port management contracts held by a company in Hong Kong were unconstitutional: the US Secretary of State claimed China could use the Panama canal as a “choke point” in the event of a conflict.
Juan Enrique Serrano, a professor specialising in Latin America-China relations at the University of Chile, warns of the chilling effect these dynamics could have on domestic policy across Latin America: “There’s an unlikely but possible scenario in which the US argues that exports of lithium from Chile to China have a dual military use, because one gram ends up in some high-end computer on a plane.” Chile is South America’s leading lithium producer.
Environmental soldiers
For environmentalists, the increasing military interest in materials associated with the energy transition raises thorny questions.
The importance of these minerals to the energy transition has led many environmentalists to see mining as a necessary evil. While organisations like Greenpeace argue demand should be reduced to limit environmental harm, they accept that some mining will be necessary.
Serra Verde says it does not use intensive mining techniques, so its operations have a “much lower impact and superior sustainability credentials”. But mining is inherently extractive, with all of the impacts on the environment and local communities that follow.
Military interest in those materials makes moderate support for extraction harder to swallow. As Global Witness puts it: “This emerging military minerals complex is the opposite of a climate solution. Rather, it will accelerate our slide towards climate catastrophe.”
Military use of critical minerals could also divert materials away from the transition. Research has suggested the 7,500 tonnes of cobalt and 50,000 tonnes of graphite the US government plans to stockpile could instead produce 100,000 electric buses.
Meanwhile, the International Institute for Environment and Development warns demand projections based on the energy transition alone are increasingly underestimating the true demand for critical minerals. This means more stress on mining areas than is currently anticipated.
Johnstone says environmental campaigners need to rekindle old alliances in this debate: “The peace movements and the green movements began as a shared thing in the 1960s and 70s [then] they drifted apart. It seems essential that those kind of coalitions come together again.”
Towards better regulation?
Johnstone believes existing sustainability frameworks are not well equipped for the current moment: “They’re all predicated on this kind of old world where sustainability is the main shared goal. They’re not really built for this world of geopolitical competition.”
Successfully protecting the energy transition from the interests of the military industrial complex will require strong regulations and global cooperation. Both were key demands in an open letter to UN delegates in July, signed by more than 100 advocacy organisations.
Monica de Bolle, a senior fellow at the nonprofit Peterson Institute for International Economics in the US, says: “Great demand exists [for rare earths], but how do we prioritise it? [We need] strong regulations, strong legal frameworks and some sort of institutional markers to be able to guide these decisions, because otherwise it’s a no man’s land.”
Latin American countries will also be wary of entering another round of extractivism in which their natural resources are extracted to the ultimate benefit of the Global North.
In September, Brazil signed a new critical minerals strategy into law focused on expanding domestic manufacturing and processing. It created the National Council for the Industrialisation of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE).
Luciano de Almeida Freitas, a legal consultant at the US law firm Carlton Fields, writes that the law opens the way for Brazil to screen foreign investments, such as for Serra Verde. But he also notes the country is behind its partners in developing processing capacity: “Mining is only the first step.” Whether Brazil remains an “extraction site”, or can hold its own downstream will determine the “difference between resource sovereignty and industrial sovereignty”.
The world has changed greatly since 1939, with climate action and new technologies like AI joining the military as drivers of industrial demand. When it comes to critical minerals, however, some are finding that little has changed.

India Plans a Critical Mineral Stockpiling Policy
India Plans Strategic Stockpiles to Secure Critical Mineral Supplies: The Ministry of Mines is preparing a policy for strategic stockpiling of critical minerals to reduce import dependence and protect Indian industries from global supply disruptions. According to the supplied report, the policy is expected to be finalised within a month.
Critical minerals are raw materials essential for economic growth, technological development and national security. Their supply may be vulnerable because of geopolitical tensions, concentrated production and limited processing facilities.
Lithium and cobalt are important for rechargeable batteries, while nickel supports battery manufacturing and industrial applications. Copper is essential for electricity networks and renewable energy infrastructure. Rare earth elements are used in wind turbines, advanced electronics and other strategic technologies.
Why India Needs Strategic Mineral Reserves
A strategic stockpile is a reserve of essential materials maintained to ensure availability during emergencies or supply disruptions. India faces several challenges in securing critical minerals.
- Import dependence: Limited domestic production and processing expose industries to international price fluctuations and supply interruptions.
- Concentrated processing capacity: China accounts for approximately 90% of global critical mineral processing capacity, according to the supplied material. This concentration creates risks for countries dependent on international supplies.
- Geopolitical tensions: Export restrictions and trade disputes can affect electric vehicles, battery manufacturing and clean-energy infrastructure.
- Overseas acquisition difficulties: Projects involving foreign mineral assets can face financial, regulatory and implementation delays.
India has pursued overseas mineral investments through Khanij Bidesh India Ltd. (KABIL). Progress has been reported in Argentina, where KABIL has acquired five lithium brine blocks in Catamarca province. Other proposed investments have faced challenges.
Static GK fact: KABIL is a joint venture of three Central Public Sector Enterprises—National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO), Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL) and Mineral Exploration and Consultancy Limited (MECL)—formed to secure critical and strategic minerals from overseas sources.
National Critical Minerals Mission
The National Critical Minerals Mission (NCMM) aims to strengthen India’s critical mineral supply chains through exploration, mining, overseas partnerships, recycling and domestic processing.
The mission proposes a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme with the following features:
| Component | Proposed provision | 
| Financial allocation for stockpiling | ₹500 crore | 
| Mission period | 2024–25 to 2030–31 | 
| Minimum mineral coverage | At least five critical minerals | 
| Institutional participation | Central PSUs and private companies | 
| Primary objective | Maintain supplies during disruptions | 
The proposed policy is expected to establish arrangements for selecting minerals, determining reserve quantities, storing materials and releasing them during emergencies.
Expanding Domestic Processing Capacity
Stockpiling offers short-term protection, but long-term security requires domestic processing capabilities and technological development. The government is considering specialised processing parks in four states to develop industrial ecosystems for particular minerals.
Such facilities could support processing infrastructure, specialised supply chains and downstream manufacturing. However, establishing them requires investment, technical expertise, skilled workers and reliable access to raw materials.
The Ministry of Mines has also identified nine Centres of Excellence to support indigenous processing technology development. A separate scheme for lithium and nickel processing has also been under consideration, given the importance of these minerals to battery manufacturing.
Static GK Tip: Mineral processing converts extracted ores or mineral-bearing materials into usable forms. Mining a mineral domestically does not automatically ensure supply security if the country still depends on overseas processing technology or facilities.
Challenges and Way Forward
India must address technological gaps, delays in overseas acquisitions and uncertainty over the implementation of strategic reserves. Effective stockpiling also requires clear institutional responsibilities, secure storage, regular replenishment and transparent release procedures.
The government should diversify international suppliers, accelerate domestic exploration, promote mineral recycling and strengthen partnerships with private industry. Indigenous research and environmentally responsible mining will also be important.
A coordinated strategy combining strategic reserves, overseas partnerships, domestic processing and technological self-reliance can help India reduce exposure to global supply shocks while supporting its clean-energy and manufacturing ambitions.

articles.title: LUBABALO CENGANI | How critical minerals are reshaping global trade realignments - Sowetan
articles.summary: LUBABALO CENGANI | How critical minerals are reshaping global trade realignments  Sowetan
articles.full_text:
For nearly half a century, the global trading architecture operated under a convenient neoliberal fiction: that open markets, low tariffs and frictionless, just-in-time supply chains were politically neutral.
Today the insatiable demand for critical minerals, from lithium and cobalt to platinum group metals (PGMs) and rare earths, has shattered that illusion.
Geopolitical strategy, state security and resource sovereignty have dethroned mere cost efficiency as the primary drivers of international commerce.
We are witnessing a profound structural fracture: global trade is fragmenting into ideologically aligned mineral blocs, while resource-rich nations across the Global South are seizing their reserves to dismantle historically extractive terms of trade and assert true industrial agency.
The 20th century trade regime was anchored in liquid hydrocarbons, with global trade lanes drawn around oil pipelines, maritime chokepoints and tanker routes dominated by Opec and Western energy majors. In contrast, the 21st century energy transition and AI hardware ecosystem rely heavily on mineral refining, chemical synthesis and metallurgy.
Unlike oil, which features relatively distributed global refining, critical mineral supply chains exhibit extreme midstream concentration risk. According to UNCTAD research, a tiny cluster of countries controls the overwhelming majority of global extraction and processing.
South Africa sits at the epicentre of this global trade realignment, holding massive reserves of manganese, chrome and PGMs essential for green hydrogen and industrial tech. However, the country faces a critical structural imperative
China, in particular, maintains a dominant market share in magnet rare earth refining, battery-grade lithium and cobalt chemical processing. From a critical analysis standpoint, this concentration has transformed refining capacity into a strategic geopolitical lever, dismantling the neoliberal premise that global supply chains naturally optimise for security and stability.
In response to structural vulnerabilities, developed economies are leveraging aggressive trade policy and state intervention to build preferential, ideologically aligned supply corridors.
Western initiatives such as the US Inflation Reduction Act, the EU Critical Raw Materials Act and the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP) FORGE platform condition tax credits, market access and state subsidies on minerals extracted or processed within “friendly” allied nations.
Consequently the World Trade Organisation’s multilateral framework is being bypassed in favour of bilateral critical mineral pacts, strategic off-take agreements and price-support mechanisms like binding price floors. This dual-bloc fragmentation replaces open multilateralism with weaponised interdependence, where trade rules are dictated by political capital rather than comparative advantage.
Historically resource-rich developing nations occupied a subordinate position in the global division of labour relegated to exporting cheap raw materials while importing expensive finished goods. Mineral-rich nations across the Global South are systematically rejecting this “extract-and-export” model. UNCTAD data highlights a sharp surge in national export bans, quotas and licensing restrictions aimed at capturing midstream value.
Indonesia imposed raw nickel export bans and moratoriums on unrefined processing plants, forcing foreign automotive and battery firms to build domestic smelters.
Zimbabwe instituted bans on raw lithium concentrate exports alongside export quotas, compelling Chinese and Western investors to process lithium sulphate locally. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) enforced cobalt export quotas to regulate market supply and capture higher battery value locally.
The critical minerals boom is not merely a resource rush; it is a fundamental rewrite of the rules of global trade, replacing neoliberal open markets with geopolitical alignment, local industrialisation and resource sovereignty
By leveraging regional blocs like the African Union (AU) and ASEAN, resource-endowed nations are coordinating trade stances to shift from passive suppliers to active industrial hubs.
South Africa sits at the epicentre of this global trade realignment, holding massive reserves of manganese, chrome and PGMs essential for green hydrogen and industrial tech. However, the country faces a critical structural imperative. It must rapidly address domestic energy reliability and rail infrastructure bottlenecks — or risk being bypassed as capital shifts toward jurisdictions capable of handling energy-intensive midstream processing.
Diplomatically, South Africa’s leadership under its G20 Presidency championing the G20 Critical Minerals Framework positioned the nation as a vital bridge. By advocating for value retention, technology transfer and equitable trade rules, South Africa is mediating between Western capital requirements and the African continent’s demand for true resource sovereignty.
The critical minerals boom is not merely a resource rush; it is a fundamental rewrite of the rules of global trade, replacing neoliberal open markets with geopolitical alignment, local industrialisation and resource sovereignty.
Under traditional market dynamics, buyers could easily substitute commodities or switch suppliers to drive down costs. Critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, manganese, PGMs and rare earths are non-substitutable hardware foundations for the green energy transition, AI data centres and advanced defence systems.
Because geological reserves are heavily concentrated in specific Global South jurisdictions, Western and East Asian industrial powerhouses face an inescapable physical reality: they cannot innovate around geography. This turns physical possession of reserves into direct geopolitical leverage.
By implementing deliberate state interventions such as raw mineral export bans, licensing quotas and processing mandates, nations like Indonesia (nickel), Zimbabwe (lithium) and the DRC (cobalt) are breaking this cycle. They are forcing multinational corporations to build refineries, smelters and manufacturing ecosystems locally as the mandatory price of admission.
Global South nations no longer must accept take-it-or-leave-it terms from a single Western-dominated market framework. Instead they can play competing powers against one another
Other African nations and several major Latin American and Southeast Asian states have implemented strict export bans, state monopolies or mandatory local processing laws to capture value. These also include:
- Ghana (lithium & bauxite);
- Chile (lithium);
- Guinea (bauxite & iron ore);
- Namibia (lithium and rare earths); and
- Mexico (lithium).
The fragmentation of global trade into competing power structures such as Western-led MSP corridors vs Chinese midstream dominance and expanded Brics networks eliminates the traditional Western monopsony.
Global South nations no longer must accept take-it-or-leave-it terms from a single Western-dominated market framework. Instead they can play competing powers against one another, demanding direct infrastructure investment, technology transfer and local equity stakes in exchange for long-term off-take access.
Historically individual developing countries were isolated and forced into a “race to the bottom” on environmental standards and royalty rates.
Today regional and multilateral platforms such as the AU’s Green Minerals Strategy, ASEAN and South Africa’s advocacy for the G20 Critical Minerals Framework enable collective bargaining.
By standardising export rules, royalty structures and local content requirements across entire regions, the Global South prevents foreign capital from pitting one mineral-rich state against another.
- Cengani is a political studies master’s graduate from Nelson Mandela University

Tanzania Poised to be East African Fossil Fuel, Critical Minerals Hub
Tanzania's finance minister says the country is nearing final agreement for a large LNG project and two critical minerals projects.
Released Wednesday, October 14, 2026
Reports related to this article:
Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)
Summary
Tanzania is gradually making moves to be a major resource conduit and producer in East Africa, gradually setting itself up to be a supplier of LNG and the critical mineral graphite.
Anticipated Finish Line
Tanzania's finance minister said agreements regarding a multibillion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility and two critical minerals projects in the country are close to happening, according to a report from Reuters. Industrial Info Resources data show more than US$82 billion worth of industrial construction lined up for Tanzania, although not all of this will occur as planned. The bulk of this spending comes from the power, mining, and fossil fuel industries.
LNG
By far the largest project on Tanzania's books is an LNG production and export facility in Lindi on the coast of the Indian Ocean. The project is headed by Shell and Equinor but features multiple minority partners, including Exxon Mobil Corporation. While a final decision had been expected this summer, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar told Reuters the final agreements are "almost there."
The LNG facility would source its gas from the country's offshore resources, specifically Block 1, which Shell acquired in its purchase of BG Group, and Block 2, which is operated by Equinor. Other partners in the LNG plant hold interests in the offshore assets, including ExxonMobil for Block 2, and Singapore-based Pavilion Energy for Block 1.
The facility is expected to have at least two production trains producing around 10 million tons per annum (MTPA) combined. While a final decision has yet to be reached on the plant, construction could begin as early as next year, putting the facility on track for an expected 2031 completion date and providing a major supply of LNG to primarily Asian markets, although Omar said some of the LNG would be used domestically. Readers can access details of the project, including anticipated construction timelines, key contact details, and equipment and service needs, by clicking here.
Major Crude Oil Export Terminal
One Tanzanian project that is certainly happening is the addition of crude oil storage capacity at an export terminal near Tanga to support the East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), which will run from oilfields in landlocked neighbor Uganda to the Tanzanian terminal on the Indian Ocean. According to an update from earlier this month by the EACOP, the pipeline is 93% complete, with first oil expected to flow in early 2027, just in time for the anticipated completion of work at the export terminal. The addition of dozens of tanks at Tanga is quite extensive, representing around 2 billion barrels of crude oil storage capacity, ready for export onto global markets.
Critical Minerals
The Tanzanian finance minister also said final agreements were nearing for two major critical minerals projects. Tanzania has major deposits of the critical mineral graphite and other critical metals and minerals such as uranium, copper, nickel and cobalt, as well as a large gold mine development that is expected to wrap up next year.
The two largest graphite mining and processing projects in the country represent more than US$500 million in combined investment value, and both have been have given a high probability (81-99%) of moving forward as planned by Industrial Info Resources. While Omar didn't name the two projects anticipated to make headway soon, he suggested that U.S. concerns were involved, and one of these two largest graphite projects is poised to change ownership to a U.S. company later this month.
The Nachu graphite-mining project in the Lindi region of southeastern Tanzania has changed ownership a couple of times since its inception, initially headed by Australia's Magnis Energy Technologies, which transferred ownership to fellow Australian company Ryzon Materials. Now a U.S. company, Sow Good, primarily known for its freeze-dried snack products, is taking over the development from Ryzon, expecting to obtain a 99.7% ownership stake in the two Ryzon companies developing the mine, and representing a new direction for the U.S. company. The deadline for the deal's finalization falls later this week.
The open pit mine and processing complex is anticipated to produce 240,000 tons per year of graphite concentrate over a 15.5-year mine life. Industrial Info Resources has been reporting on the project since 2014, with the originally anticipated construction start slipping over the years, but the change in ownership could suggest movement on the project soon. Once started, construction is anticipated to last around two years.
Australian firm Black Rock Mining is behind another significant Tanzanian graphite development in the Morogoro region in the country's south-central interior. While some site preparation for the above-ground mine has begun and certain early-work contracts are in place, Black Rock has yet to make a firm final investment decision (FID) on the project's construction, taking into account the availability of power resources, port infrastructure and transport access. With an initial earth-moving contract in place, a positive FID could see work beginning in earnest this year, putting the facility on track to begin ramping up toward full production of around 89,000 tons per year of graphite concentrate around two years later.
Power
Such large LNG and mining concerns require a solid power base, and Tanzania has plans to increase its power generation. In August, the country reported that its generation capacity had reached more than 4,600 megawatts, and it aims to have 8,000 MW of capacity in place by 2030, largely from renewable energy resources. The country has multiple power projects lined up, with geothermal and hydropower representing the two largest fuel types for the proposed plants.
Key Takeaways
- According to Tanzania's finance minister, the country is expecting to reach final agreements soon on a large Indian Ocean LNG export terminal and two critical minerals projects.
- Tanzania also is expanding its port infrastructure in Tanga to allow for exports of Ugandan oil carried on the upcoming East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline.
- The pipeline is reportedly 93% complete according to a report from earlier this month, while the LNG project and two significant graphite mining projects have yet to the full green light.

OPEC+ is reportedly set to keep oil production quotas unchanged in November as the Iran war continues to disrupt output across the Persian Gulf.
The decision comes as crude prices push back toward $100 a barrel and diesel prices hit records, with the supply shock prompting the Group of Seven to coordinate a massive emergency stock release.
The seven-member OPEC+ subgroup led by Saudi Arabia and Russia has reached an agreement in principle to keep November production targets unchanged, delegates told Bloomberg ahead of Sunday’s video conference, where the decision is expected to be finalized.
The move would follow the group’s existing production roadmap. OPEC+ had already signaled that it would pause further quota increases through the end of 2026, after implementing modest production increases during the six months through August.
The latest increases had largely been symbolic in terms of actual market supply, with the Iran war disrupting production and exports across the Persian Gulf.
The conflict has left output from major OPEC producers, including Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait, significantly below prewar levels, limiting the practical impact of the group’s quota decisions.
OPEC+ is expected to settle its broader 2027 production policy at a full ministerial meeting in November.
The OPEC+ decision comes as governments move to counter the growing fuel-supply squeeze.
President Donald Trump said that the U.S. will not impose a proposed diesel export ban after the “Group of Seven” nations agreed to coordinate the release of 100 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products from emergency reserves.
The release will begin immediately and run for four months, with the G7 saying a “substantial” amount of diesel will reach the market during the first 20 days.
Trump had repeatedly floated restricting U.S. diesel exports as European fuel supplies came under pressure following disruptions to Gulf production.
“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.
The G7 also committed to avoiding energy and energy-product export restrictions between member nations and urged other oil-producing countries to avoid measures that could further tighten global supplies.
The group said it will coordinate the releases through the International Energy Agency and could discuss additional diesel releases if market conditions deteriorate further.
The emergency action follows the IEA's record 400-million-barrel coordinated stock release in March, underscoring the scale of the supply shock facing global energy markets.
Crude oil prices were mixed last week, with the U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures expiring in November falling 1.41% to $91.26 a barrel after a 3.82% fall the week before. However, Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 3.47% this week, hovering around $102.72 a barrel after a 0.46% increase the week before.

This was 903,000 barrels more than in August, according to OPEC's monthly report. The increase occurred despite disruptions to oil transportation through the Strait of Hormuz, which OPEC linked to the war with Iran.
Saudi Arabia increased production
OPEC member countries increased production by approximately 920,000 barrels per day, to 25.097 million barrels. At the same time, production by countries outside OPEC that participate in the OPEC+ agreement fell by approximately 18,000 barrels per day.
Saudi Arabia posted the largest production increase. According to data provided by the kingdom, its output rose from 6.238 million barrels per day in August to 8.372 million in September — by more than 2 million barrels. Under the take-or-pay agreement, Trafigura will purchase 100 000 t of battery-grade lithium products from EnergyX over a 10 year term.

The agreement covers lithium products from both of EnergyX’s first two flagship projects with lithium carbonate supplied from Black Giant™ in Chile and lithium hydroxide from Project Lonestar™ in Texas. A significant share will be directed to the US battery supply chain.
Trafigura’s offtake agreement is a turning point for EnergyX. The company has proven its technology in the lab, at pilot scale, and now at the company’s demonstration plants in both its US and Chile projects, each of which is the largest DLE plant in its respective country. The agreement builds on EnergyX’s recent financing momentum, including Eni’s US$225 million strategic investment in Project Black Giant in Chile and a US$690 million Letter of Intent from the US EXIM Bank to provide debt financing for the project.
“Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” said Teague Egan, Founder and CEO of EnergyX. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product. It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.”
EnergyX’s production will be powered by its proprietary GET-Lit™ direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology platform, which is covered by more than 150 patents. EnergyX commissioned Project Lonestar, the largest DLE lithium production plant in the US, in Texas in April 2026. The company is advancing commercial-scale projects across North and South America, including the 52 500 tpy Project Black Giant in Chile and its Smackover operations in Texas and Arkansas.

articles.title: EIB Canada Critical Minerals Deal Heads to Montreal Summit as Trump Tariffs Cede Advantage - Tech Times
articles.summary: EIB Canada Critical Minerals Deal Heads to Montreal Summit as Trump Tariffs Cede Advantage  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Canada and the European Union are poised to announce the most significant realignment of Western critical minerals architecture in years — a deal that would, for the first time, allow the European Investment Bank to directly fund Canadian mining projects, with an EIB-Canada letter of intent already signed at the PDAC 2026 conference. The agreement, confirmed in a draft joint statement circulated among EU member states and reported by AFP and POLITICO, was reached in the weeks bracketed by two converging crises: US tariffs that have fractured Canada's southern trade anchor, and a Chinese rare-earth accommodation reached October 9 under the EU-China rare-earth licensing framework that illustrated, even as it briefly eased, how much administrative leverage Beijing retains over European industrial supply chains.
For Ottawa and Brussels alike, the pact — to be formally unveiled at the October 29–30 summit in Montreal, 17 days from publication — represents something beyond a bilateral minerals deal. It is insurance against an uncertain era of great-power competition, and a structural bet on Canadian geology as the West's most accessible hedge against Chinese dominance of the materials that power both clean energy and modern defense systems.
Six-Year Push Toward EIB Financing Reaches Decisive Moment
The foundations stretch back to June 2021, when the EIB and Canada signed an EIB-Canada raw materials partnership — a framework that sat largely dormant until shifting geopolitics forced both sides to act. The pace accelerated sharply in March 2026, when the EIB and Canada formalized a Letter of Intent at PDAC alongside a broader EU-Canada Joint Statement on Critical Minerals.
That same week, Canada's Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson announced 30 new critical minerals partnerships expected to unlock C$12.1 billion (approximately $8.51 billion USD) in project capital across 12 allied partners. The announcements brought the total mobilized under Canada's Critical Minerals Production Alliance to C$18.5 billion (approximately $13.0 billion USD).
The March letter of intent, while significant diplomatically, stopped well short of a concrete financing commitment. What changed in the months since was not the minerals themselves — but the world around them. By early October 2026, the draft joint statement for the Montreal summit indicated that both sides had moved decisively further. The document states that Canada and the EIB have "completed negotiations of an agreement that will facilitate European Investment in critical Canadian resources, in particular, critical minerals." That phrase — "completed negotiations" — marks a decisive step beyond the 2026 letter of intent, signaling that EIB financing for specific Canadian projects is no longer hypothetical.
As EIB President Calviño told CBC, "the time is ripe" to deepen cooperation with Canada by exploring how to finance Canadian projects. She identified critical minerals as the first area of shared interest and said the EIB was exploring a framework agreement enabling investment "and beyond" — language that signals ambitions extending into digital and clean-energy infrastructure, echoing the agenda Prime Minister Mark Carney laid before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on September 17.
Montreal Summit Package: "Alliance for Future" Extends Beyond Minerals
The critical minerals agreement is the centerpiece of a broader package expected to be unveiled at the Montreal summit, framed under what the draft joint statement calls an "Alliance for the Future." The package includes a digital trade deal designed to "allow for faster, lower cost secure digital trade and transactions," an agreement to strengthen cooperation between competition authorities, and a pact for the EU and Canada to jointly purchase 50 water bombers made by Canadian firm De Havilland for wildfire deployment by 2030. The document also calls for strategic stockpiles of critical resources to shield supply chains from "market fluctuations and geopolitical impacts."
The summit follows European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's Canada EU associate membership proposal that Canada be invited to become the EU's first-ever "associate member" — a category invented for one country, including access to EU defense-industrial cooperation, Horizon Europe research programs, and Erasmus+ exchanges.
For Prime Minister Carney, the Montreal summit represents the operationalization of a pivot he outlined in Strasbourg. In his Carney Strasbourg address on strategic autonomy, Carney said Canada and Europe should "secure our strategic autonomy" through cooperation in "critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments" — explicitly linking rare-earth supply chains to digital sovereignty and sovereign compute infrastructure in a single strategic frame. Carney's Canada AI for All strategy — a C$2 billion initiative targeting AI adoption growth from 12% to 60% of Canadian businesses by 2034 — positions Canada as a producer not only of raw minerals but of the digital infrastructure those minerals ultimately enable.
EIB President Calviño has publicly committed the EIB to injecting €70 billion (approximately $78.6 billion USD) into European technology infrastructure, including AI gigafactories built in partnership with the European Commission. The Canada-EIB deal is therefore embedded in a broader European technology-sovereignty push that extends well past mine gates.
Trump Tariffs Force Canada to Seek European Market Insurance
The proximate cause of the acceleration is unmistakable. Trump 50% tariffs on Canada — covering steel, aluminum, automobiles, and car parts — have fundamentally altered Ottawa's strategic calculus, pushing Canada to seek what analysts call "alternate market insurance": locking in European offtake commitments and financing that reduce dependence on the US as a buyer of Canadian mineral output.
US Trade Representative confirmation that Trump's tariff regime will not change has removed any expectation of near-term restoration of the prior trade architecture. The collapse of US-Canada trade talks left Ottawa with sharply reduced leverage in Washington and sharply increased incentive in Brussels.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, among the most vocal Canadian politicians on the minerals file, captured the dynamic bluntly in his Ford statement on critical minerals: "At a time when China is winning the race to dominate these resources while also restricting the sale and shipment of critical minerals to the US, Canada and Ontario need to urgently get our critical minerals out of the ground, processed and shipped to the factory floors that are building for the future."
Rare Earth Exchanges, which first reported the EIB-Canada pact's finalization on October 11, noted that European financing and offtake commitments could redirect Canadian critical mineral output toward EU reindustrialization — a development that would complicate US defense supply chain security even as Washington simultaneously seeks preferential access to those same resources.
China's Rare-Earth Controls: One-Year Licensing Deal Masks Structural Risk
If US tariff pressure is the push, China's dominance in critical mineral processing is the pull. The October 9 EU-China licensing framework illustrated why both sides feel urgency acutely — and why a one-year diplomatic accommodation is not the same as long-term supply security.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič met Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing and confirmed the EU is working with China on an EU-China rare-earth export system to ensure more stable flows of rare-earth minerals to the bloc. Brussels called for "a new and stable system of trade in critical materials" — language that acknowledged the framework does not eliminate Chinese administrative discretion but rather regularizes it.
That distinction matters enormously. A licensing system that must be renewed annually preserves Beijing's ability to slow-walk applications, impose retroactive conditions, or decline licenses for individual buyers as geopolitical circumstances change. It is structurally different from a trade agreement that permanently removes export controls, and EU leaders know it.
The numbers underlying that vulnerability are stark, as documented in the Library of Parliament supply chain data:
- China accounts for 69% of total world mine production of rare-earth elements
- China accounts for 79% of total world mine production of graphite
- In 2024, China's share of refined material production reached 96% for graphite, 91% for rare earths, 78% for cobalt, 70% for lithium, and 44% for copper
European Commission President von der Leyen noted that China's tightening of export controls "has a huge impact on us here in the European Union," adding that the bloc will focus on "joint purchasing, stockpiling, and investment in strategic projects for the production and processing of critical raw materials here in the EU."
The EU Critical Raw Materials Act — which sets a target of no more than 65% of any strategic material from a single country — cannot be met at current Western production levels without Canadian capacity coming online at scale. The Canada pact is the most direct near-term mechanism Brussels has to move that needle.
Canada's Offer: Only Western Hemisphere Nation With Full EV Battery Mineral Set
Canada's attractiveness as a partner rests on a combination of geological endowment, political stability, democratic governance, and sheer proximity. Canada holds all EV battery minerals required for battery manufacturing — graphite, nickel, aluminum, lithium, copper, cobalt, manganese, molybdenum, and rare earth elements — making it the only country in the Western Hemisphere with this full set. Canada is also home to 45 advanced Canadian mineral projects spanning graphite, lithium, and rare earth elements across multiple provinces.
