articles.title: China's October Industrial Doctrine Formalizes Rare Earth Leverage: EU Secured Managed Access - Tech Times
articles.summary: China's October Industrial Doctrine Formalizes Rare Earth Leverage: EU Secured Managed Access  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
On October 9, 2026, the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council issued joint guidelines codifying Beijing's strategic "feedback loop" doctrine. That doctrine is the logic by which critical mineral processing control flows into manufacturing dominance, then into research funding, then into next-generation technology competitiveness, and it was now enshrined at the highest level of Chinese state authority. The same day, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič concluded Beijing negotiations with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and announced a package of trade understandings that, examined precisely, gave Europe access to the licensing system China controls rather than a path out of the dependency that system produces.
The headline figures from the talks were real: Chinese tariff reductions on approximately €4 billion in European goods covering car parts, olive oil, and footwear (approximately $4.49 billion); a cap on Chinese hybrid vehicle export growth to the EU; and China's commitment to continue expediting rare earth export license approvals through an existing fast-track mechanism. China did not eliminate its export controls on rare earths. It agreed only to continue processing the applications it already administers, through a mechanism it operates at its own discretion. EU Trade Commissioner Šefčovič called it a "crucial first step" toward rebalancing the relationship. The EU trade deficit with China had widened to roughly €1 billion (approximately $1.12 billion) per day in 2025. Šefčovič described it as "a mountain of a challenge."
What the October Guidelines Actually Formalize
The October 9 document covers five reform areas: advancing scientific and technological innovation; deepening the integration of science-and-technology with industrial innovation; innovating development approaches; promoting institutional and mechanism reform; and improving talent development. Nineteen specific measures span the sectors Beijing has identified as strategically critical: next-generation information technology, new energy, advanced materials, intelligent connected vehicles, robotics, biomedicine, high-end equipment, and aerospace. This is the full stack of what Beijing calls "new quality productive forces," a concept President Xi Jinping first coined during a September 2023 visit to Heilongjiang Province, and formally elevated to the top of the State Council agenda in March 2024.
The strategy is embedded in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, 2026 to 2030, which identified new quality productive forces as a key strategic task. Of the plan's 109 major projects, 28 (or 25.7 percent) are tied directly to this concept, a concentration of national planning priority in a single strategic framework without recent precedent in Chinese industrial planning. The guidelines also include an accountability provision prohibiting "improper use of policies in the name of developing new quality productive forces," signaling that Beijing is as concerned about speculative overcapacity as capability building, and will hold regional officials accountable for losses from what it calls "blind investment."
Beijing Formalizes the Feedback Loop: Critical Mineral Control as State Doctrine
For technology and supply chain analysts, the central significance of the October 9 document is that it formally codifies the strategic logic that has driven Chinese industrial policy for over a decade: controlling the processing of critical minerals, the bottleneck stage between raw ore extraction and commercially usable advanced material, provides the foundation for domestic manufacturing advantages. Those advantages generate revenue and knowledge to fund research and development, which produces next-generation competitive advantages in technology, which in turn reinforces the strategic value of Chinese-controlled mineral supply chains. This framing was first reported by Rare Earth Exchanges in its analysis of the October 9 directive.
What is new is that this logic is now the explicit, publicly stated doctrine of the two highest organs of Chinese state authority, issued in a joint formal directive. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology signaled the broader industrial arc in August 2026, when an MIIT official outlined the ministry's 2026 to 2030 raw materials strategy at the National Raw Materials Industry Symposium in Ningbo. The official framed the goal as moving China's position from "leading in scale" to "comprehensive leadership," treating minerals not as isolated commodities but as integrated components of a system linking extraction through advanced manufacturing to downstream value capture, according to Skillings Mining Review. The October 9 CPC/State Council guidelines are the political capstone of that strategy.
China's position at the top of this feedback loop is substantial. By current estimates, China controls approximately 60 to 70 percent of global rare earth mine production and over 90 percent of separation and processing capacity. That processing dominance is the critical technological bottleneck, because mining ore is meaningless without the ability to transform it into the pure elemental oxides and alloys that technology manufacturing requires. China produces approximately 93 percent of global permanent magnet output. Before export controls reshaped trade flows, China accounted for roughly 80 percent of global gallium production. Gallium is the feedstock for gallium nitride semiconductors used in 5G base stations, military radar, and electric power electronics.
How Does China's Rare Earth Control Translate to Real Supply Chain Risk?
The supply chain risk runs through three distinct channels, each with a different timeline.
The first is direct material availability. China imposed April 2025 export controls on seven rare earth elements during the escalating trade conflict with the United States, before implementing a temporary suspension of a second wave of controls in late 2025. That suspension will expire on November 10, 2026. If Beijing reinstates those controls, European and American manufacturers of electric motors, wind turbines, MRI machines, defense systems, and precision-guided munitions will face restricted access to materials for which no viable short-term alternative supply chain currently exists at the required scale.
The second channel is processing capacity concentration. Even when sufficient rare earth ore can be mined outside China (Australia's Lynas Rare Earths and MP Materials in California both produce significant concentrates), the ore must be separated and refined into the specific elemental forms manufacturers require. China controls approximately 90 percent of global heavy rare earth separation capacity. Non-Chinese rare earth concentrates were trading at estimated premiums of 15 to 25 percent over Chinese-origin equivalents purely for supply security, a market signal of how acute the processing constraint is perceived to be.
The third channel is technology leverage. The October 9 guidelines push artificial intelligence, quantum technology, and robotics alongside advanced materials within a single integrated policy framework. The implication, now official state doctrine, is that whoever controls the mineral feedstock influences the pace of development in AI hardware, next-generation defense systems, and clean energy equipment.
EU-China Trade Talks: Same Day, Same Leverage
The October 9 talks marked the second meeting of the EU-China TIC mechanism established in June 2026. Brussels had set October as a deadline for tangible progress, driven partly by concern about the approaching November 2026 expiry of China's rare earth export control suspension. The EU Critical Raw Materials Act, enacted May 2024, sets 2030 targets requiring that at least 10 percent of EU annual strategic mineral consumption be extracted domestically, 40 percent processed domestically, 25 percent recovered from recycled materials, and that no single country supply more than 65 percent of any strategic material.
What the EU received from October 9 was meaningful in the near term and structurally limited in the longer term. China's commitment to continue fast-tracking license approvals does not create new supply capacity, does not reduce the EU's near-total import dependency on Chinese rare earth magnets (an estimated 98 percent of EU industry consumption), and does not set binding commitments on license volumes or processing timelines. A third TIC round planned for March 2027. The October 9 guidelines, published the same day negotiations concluded, make explicit that China's domestic capability will continue to be built regardless of trade negotiation outcomes.
Brussels's October Deal Echoes the WTO Quota Model That Europe Already Fought Once
The most significant dimension of the EU's October 9 outcome is one the official statements do not mention: the fast-track licensing arrangement is structurally similar to the rare earth export quota system China administered from 2009 to 2014. Under that earlier framework, Beijing controlled the quantity of rare earth materials available to global markets through annual quotas, giving Chinese domestic manufacturers preferential access while foreign buyers competed for constrained supply. WTO ruled against China in a dispute brought jointly by the European Union, United States, and Japan in 2014, finding that the export restrictions violated China's WTO accession commitments.
China complied with the 2014 ruling by eliminating the formal quota mechanism. But what followed was not meaningful supply chain diversification. It was a decade in which Chinese rare earth prices fell after quota elimination, reducing the economic justification for investment in alternative processing capacity outside China. articles.full_text:
Aadya Chaturvedi, “Domestic Refining of Critical Minerals: India’s Next Petroleum Story,” ORF Issue Brief No. 901, Observer Research Foundation, October 2026.
As temperatures rise to unsustainable levels, the urgency to adopt emerging technologies—such as electric vehicles, solar panels, and wind turbines—has become more apparent in evolving national priorities. These technologies present wide-ranging and unprecedented ramifications for economic growth, energy sovereignty, and national security.
In turn, they require massive amounts of critical minerals, such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, silicon, and rare earth elements (REEs). True to their name, critical minerals have more complex supply chains than those of other ‘non-critical’ minerals. Although they are no more geographically constrained than resources such as oil and natural gas, they require advanced capabilities for extraction, processing, and refining. Their midstream value chains are concentrated in countries that do not necessarily possess abundant reserves. Over the past few decades, countries such as China and Finland have established a lead in the processing and refining of minerals such as nickel and cobalt, respectively,[1] despite lacking commercially viable domestic reserves. Long-term off-take partnerships with resource-rich countries, continuous research and development (R&D) of sophisticated refining methods, and integration with downstream industries have enabled them to establish a strong position in these value chains.
India has set ambitious targets for its energy transition. As per its Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement, it aims to achieve 60 percent cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil fuel-based energy resources by 2035.[2] This would require the rapid integration of emerging critical technologies into the domestic market. However, India remains heavily import-dependent for both components and minerals. At a time when critical minerals are increasingly being used to secure specific geoeconomic outcomes—for instance, China’s export controls on REEs in response to United States (US) tariffs[3]—it is important for India to secure its supply chains.
While India is progressively building a base for the manufacturing and assembly of solar wafers, wind towers, cathodes, advanced chemistry batteries, and integrated circuits, efforts to secure the supply of minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel have lagged. Recent initiatives such as the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Acts 2023 and 2025 aim to give a push to domestic exploration, but are not enough to build a sizeable stockpile in the short term, as mine development lead times can be up to 20 years.[4] Although the recovery of important minerals from end-of-life products is an emerging alternative, the lack of commercialisation of requisite technologies and economies of scale makes this a viable solution only in the medium to long term.[5] However, refining is a stage in the value chain where India can make a place for itself.
India has experience in refining minerals for which it does not possess abundant domestic reserves. Following economic liberalisation in the 1990s, it commenced refining heavy-sour crude imported from West Asia and has recently augmented its capacity to even process medium-sour Russian crude. It has built the chemistries, infrastructure, and skills to lay the foundation of a refining ecosystem, becoming the third-largest oil refiner worldwide.[6] Furthermore, India already refines seven of the 30 critical minerals it has identified.[7] However, these capacities have yet to achieve economies of scale, and there is no coherent framework for augmenting domestic refining capacity.
Refined products capture a large share of the value chain, commanding prices three to four times higher than raw ores.[8] However, refineries may operate on thin margins due to feedstock price volatility. Lithium prices began declining in late 2022,[9] while cobalt and nickel prices fell in 2023 and 2024, respectively,[10],[11] amidst market oversupply. While this compressed margins, the impact was more acute at the primary processing stage than at the intermediate chemicals refining stage.[12] This brief argues for building a domestic base exactly at this stage. From an economic standpoint, refining domestically is advantageous for capital expenditure (CAPEX) and cost efficiency.[13] It will also boost the growth of downstream industries such as battery manufacturing and assembly. Domestic refining also shields value chains against global shocks and geopolitical flux.
Figure 1: Lithium Value Chain
Source: Author’s own, using various sources.[14]
Lithium mining is dominated by Australia (spodumene rocks), Chile, and China (salt brines), which together account for 61 percent of global production.[15] Lithium extracted from brine is processed near mining sites and refined in host countries to produce lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), which is used to produce cathodes for lithium-ion phosphate (LFP) batteries. Concentrates derived from spodumene are exported for refining into lithium hydroxide (LiOH) or Li2CO3, the former being used in cathodes for nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries. China controls 62 percent of the lithium refining market.[16]
Figure 2: Cobalt Value Chain
Source: Author’s own, using various sources.[17]
Cobalt is primarily mined as a by-product of copper or nickel. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) (Kinshasa) alone holds 62 percent of the global cobalt production.[18] Hydrometallurgical processing is used to produce intermediate chemicals, such as cobalt hydroxide, which are exported and refined into battery-grade materials such as cobalt sulphate. China accounts for 78 percent of the global cobalt-refining capacity, followed by Finland, which holds 6 percent.[19]
Figure 3: Nickel Value Chain
Source: Author’s own, using various sources.[20]
Nickel’s end use depends on the type of ore from which it is extracted: laterite ores are primarily used in stainless-steel production, while sulphide ores are crucial for nickel-chemistry batteries and renewable-energy technologies. Given that stainless steel is used to manufacture batteries and renewables, securing the supply chains of both ores is vital. Indonesia controls 67 percent of global nickel production but dominates in laterite ores, while sulphide ores are concentrated in Australia and Canada.[21] While Indonesia (45 percent) dominates the refining of laterite ores, Russia (3 percent) and Canada (4 percent) take the lead in sulphide-ore refining.[22]
Processing and refining sulphide ores typically produce Class 1 nickel, while laterite ores yield intermediate chemicals, such as nickel matte and mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP). MHP is preferred for export because it contains both nickel and cobalt and does not require hydrogen sulphide for refining,[a] allowing for cost savings.[23] These intermediate chemicals are exported for further refining to produce nickel sulphate, which is a precursor material for batteries. This part of the value chain is dominated by China.[24]
Emboldened by a wave of resource nationalism shaping contemporary geopolitics, several critical-mineral-producing countries have instituted restrictions on their exports. While Indonesia and Zimbabwe have banned the export of nickel and lithium, respectively,[25],[26] Congo has put strict quotas on cobalt exports.[27] These policies aim to compel refiners to shift operations to resource-producing countries, enabling the latter to extract maximum value domestically. China, for instance, has already established nickel-processing plants in Indonesia,[28] which was previously a leading supplier of raw nickel to the country.
The implications of these export controls, however, vary by mineral. In the case of lithium, pressure on supply chains will be limited, given that Zimbabwe is not a major producer. On the other hand, Congo’s strict export quotas are being allotted only to existing mining companies on the basis of historic production and export performance.[29] They restrict the export of crude cobalt (cobalt hydroxide), which is the backbone of the offshore refining regime.[30] Consequently, China’s cobalt hydroxide imports fell by 89.9 percent year-on-year in 2025.[31] Indonesia’s ban on nickel ores and concentrates, however, permits the export of MHP and matte, keeping these refining value chains operational.
These export controls do not necessarily narrow the window of opportunity; rather, they shift it. Countries will have to double down on diversification not only of host countries but also of feedstock. Leading producers such as Australia, Canada, and Argentina have emerged as alternative exporters. This is advantageous for India as it has commenced several mineral partnerships with these countries. Moreover, India will have to employ a strategy of importing a mix of ore concentrates and intermediate chemicals, as discussed in the next sections.
Around the turn of the millennium, rising digitisation and consumerism drove demand for electronics, and consequently, for critical minerals used to manufacture batteries and cells for mobile phones and laptops. In the 2010s, demand grew further with the introduction of electric vehicles, which accelerated the transition towards clean technologies. Countries such as China and Finland started importing ores and concentrates from resource-rich but processing-poor countries to refine them into higher-value, battery-grade chemicals. Since the 2020s, South Korea has also progressively expanded its domestic lithium-processing capabilities.

TELF AG on US technological evolution in the critical minerals sector
The future of the critical minerals industry may depend increasingly on technological capabilities rather than geological abundance alone. As Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG, emphasizes, the ability to identify, recover, and process mineral resources efficiently is becoming a decisive factor in determining their industrial and economic significance.
Key takeaway: The US Department of Energy's allocation of approximately $29.5 million to 17 research projects reflects a growing focus on advanced technologies for mineral identification, extraction, and processing. From autonomous robotics to microwave-assisted rock fragmentation, these initiatives could improve operational efficiency and influence the competitiveness of critical mineral supply chains.
The initiative also highlights a broader change in how mineral resources are evaluated. The presence of valuable materials beneath the surface remains essential, but their commercial importance depends on the technical and economic conditions required to transform them into usable products.
Why Are Technological Capabilities Becoming More Important Than Geological Abundance?
Technological capabilities are becoming increasingly important because the presence of mineral resources does not automatically guarantee their commercial availability. Advanced identification, separation, and processing techniques can influence recovery rates, operating costs, and the economic feasibility of deposits, potentially changing the competitive position of countries and industrial operators.
Several factors explain this transformation:
- Geological complexity: Some deposits contain valuable minerals in concentrations or formations that are difficult to process.
- Processing requirements: Industrial applications often require materials to meet specific purity and quality standards.
- Energy consumption: Certain processing stages demand substantial quantities of electricity.
- Recovery efficiency: Technological improvements can increase the proportion of valuable materials obtained from available resources.
- Economic competitiveness: Lower operational costs can improve the commercial attractiveness of mineral projects.
The interaction between these factors is becoming increasingly relevant for critical minerals such as lithium, copper, nickel, cobalt, vanadium, and rare earth elements.
In many cases, the principal challenge is not simply locating additional resources, but developing more effective methods for transforming existing geological materials into commercially useful products.
"The strategic importance of a mineral deposit cannot be evaluated exclusively through its size or geological characteristics. The technologies available to identify, separate, and process its components may ultimately determine how much industrial value can be generated from it," says Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.
How Could US Research Funding Accelerate Mineral Technology Development?
The US Department of Energy's approximately $29.5 million allocation supports 17 research projects designed to improve mineral production technologies. Conducted through national laboratories and federal research capabilities, these initiatives address challenges involving geological characterization, operational efficiency, material separation, and the recovery of valuable metals from complex resources.
The research priorities include:
- Accelerating mineral identification through advanced sensing technologies.
- Improving the selection of mineral-rich material before processing.
- Reducing energy requirements during rock fragmentation.
- Developing innovative techniques for recovering metals from residues.
- Investigating alternative methods for accessing underground resources.
The distinguishing feature of this initiative is its emphasis on improving the technical performance of mineral production processes.
Rather than relying exclusively on the discovery of new deposits, the research aims to identify opportunities for obtaining greater value from available geological resources.
If successfully developed and commercialized, these technologies could support more efficient domestic production while expanding the range of materials considered economically recoverable.
How Are Artificial Intelligence and Robotics Transforming Mineral Identification?
Artificial intelligence and robotics could transform mineral identification by enabling faster geological surveys, more precise material characterization, and automated analysis of underground environments. When combined with advanced sensing systems, these technologies may reduce the time required to identify valuable minerals and improve decisions about subsequent processing operations.
One research project focuses on an autonomous robotic platform equipped with hyperspectral sensors and artificial intelligence.
Hyperspectral imaging captures information across numerous wavelengths, allowing researchers to identify certain minerals according to their distinctive spectral characteristics.
By integrating this technology with robotic equipment, researchers aim to accelerate geological characterization in underground environments.
Some surveys that traditionally require days or weeks of manual activity could potentially be completed in minutes, depending on operational conditions and the capabilities of the system.
Another project combines intelligent sensors with automated analysis to distinguish mineral-rich rocks from less valuable material.
This approach could improve the selection of material entering processing facilities, potentially reducing unnecessary treatment and associated energy consumption.
"One of the most promising aspects of digital innovation is its capacity to improve decisions at the earliest stages of mineral production. Better geological information and more accurate material selection could generate efficiency improvements throughout the entire processing chain," explains Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.
Why Is Microwave-Assisted Rock Fragmentation Attracting Research Interest?
Microwave-assisted fragmentation is attracting research interest because it could reduce the energy required to break down certain types of rock. By exposing geological material to microwave energy before mechanical treatment, researchers aim to weaken its internal structure and improve the efficiency of subsequent crushing and grinding operations.
This technology focuses on comminution, the process through which large rock fragments are progressively reduced into smaller particles.
Comminution is an essential stage in many mineral processing operations because valuable minerals often need to be liberated from surrounding material before separation.
However, the process can also require substantial energy.
Microwave treatment could potentially create internal stresses within rock formations, making certain materials easier to fragment.
The effectiveness of this approach depends on mineral composition, rock properties, equipment design, and energy requirements.
Its industrial significance will depend on whether improvements in fragmentation efficiency can outweigh the additional costs of microwave treatment.
Can Innovative Recovery Technologies Unlock Value From Mineral Residues?
Innovative recovery technologies could make mineral residues more economically valuable by enabling the recovery of metals that conventional processing methods leave behind. Research involving induction heating, biological techniques, and electrochemical processes is investigating ways to recover useful materials from complex or previously processed resources.
These approaches are particularly relevant to metals such as copper, nickel, and cobalt.
Mining residues can contain quantities of valuable materials that were not recovered during initial processing.
Their commercial potential depends on several factors, including metal concentration, chemical composition, treatment costs, and prevailing market prices.
Advanced recovery methods could improve the economic feasibility of processing certain residues, potentially increasing resource availability without requiring equivalent quantities of newly developed deposits.
Could Technological Innovation Change the Economics of Critical Minerals?
Technological innovation could change critical mineral economics by lowering processing costs, improving recovery rates, and expanding the range of commercially viable resources. These developments may influence project profitability, investment decisions, and supply chain competitiveness, although their impact will depend on successful industrial implementation.
For example, a deposit with relatively low mineral concentrations may become economically attractive if new technologies reduce the costs of separating valuable components.
Similarly, improvements in recovery efficiency could increase the quantity of marketable material obtained from the same geological resource.
This possibility has important implications for global supply chains.
Countries with strong technological capabilities may be able to improve domestic mineral production even when their geological resources are comparatively limited or technically challenging.
"The economic boundaries of mineral production are not necessarily fixed. As processing technologies evolve, resources that currently present substantial technical or financial challenges could become more accessible, potentially opening new opportunities for industrial development," concludes Stanislav Kondrashov, founder of TELF AG.

articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct 15: As countries, including India, come together to tap rare earth sources and cut their dependence on China, they are becoming somewhat wary of Beijing’s weaponisation of critical minerals, according to a new report.
China controls 90 per cent of global processing and refining capacity of rare earths, which gives it ample leverage over the US and its allies.
Last year, Beijing demonstrated this when it rolled out rare earth export controls in response to US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, according to the report in World Politics Review.
Western nations wary of China's dominance
“The United States and Europe have been caught flat-footed in recent years by China’s actual and threatened use of export controls over critical minerals and related magnets,” the report warned.
Moreover, the “forcefulness and success of China’s moves on rare earths” have led some Western officials to “accuse Beijing of a decades-long scheme to place a boot on the neck of the global economy”.
China seeks control over global industry
Meanwhile, China has become geopolitically more ambitious, with its objective no longer merely to dominate rare earth production at home but also control the global industry by deciding which countries receive the technology, technicians and market access required to compete.
Jack Lifton, Co-Chair, Critical Minerals Institute (CMI), wrote in an article in Investor News recently that China’s strategies for Malaysia and Indonesia are clear indicators of this new policy.
Malaysia's rare earth strategy
Malaysia has prohibited exports of its unprocessed rare earth material, stressing domestic value addition while inviting both Chinese and non-Chinese investment. Since then, Malaysia’s non-Chinese industrial base has become more formidable.
China does not want Malaysia simply to become a Western or Japanese-sponsored competitor. It wants Malaysia to become a multi-aligned processing centre in which China remains an indispensable participant, said the article.
Also Watch:
Indonesia explores strategic mineral resources
The article also highlighted that Indonesia wants to develop rare earth resources, but there is much less public evidence that China has yet to establish a major, dedicated rare earth separation or magnet project there. Indonesia announced in February 2026 that it had identified eight prospective blocks containing rare earths and other strategic minerals.

articles.full_text:
Critical minerals are essential to the clean energy transition, digital technologies, and defence, yet global supply chains remain highly concentrated.In this article, originally published in Policy Magazine, HCSS Strategic Advisor Peter Handley explores how Canada and Europe can strengthen critical minerals supply chains through closer cooperation. As Europe seeks to strengthen its strategic autonomy and Canada looks to diversify its trade partnerships, the key lies in the midstream: processing, refining, and recycling critical minerals. By combining Canada’s abundant resources and low-carbon energy with Europe’s industrial expertise and demand, both partners can build more resilient, sustainable, and secure transatlantic supply chains.
Originally published in Policy Magazine, August 5th, 2026
Since 2025, Canada and the European Union have tightened the ties of the transatlantic relationship across a number of metrics, from trade to defence to the Eurovision Song Contest. Among those metrics is the securing of reliable and sustainable critical minerals supply chains.
When the European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) entered into force in May 2024, one number mentioned in the act did more than any other to concentrate minds in European capitals: 40 per cent.
By 2030, the Act says, the EU’s processing capacity should be able to cover at least 40 per cent of its own annual consumption of strategic raw materials, alongside targets of 10 per cent domestic extraction, 25 per cent recycling, and no more than 65 per cent from a single third country.
Two years on, that benchmark is the best lens through which Canada can view Europe’s critical minerals strategy, because it names the stage of the value chain where both partners have the most to gain from expansion and from working together: the midstream, where the processing, refining, and chemical- transformation steps of that value chain bridge the gap between raw mining (upstream) and manufacturing (downstream).
The EU’s 40% benchmark did not emerge from nowhere. Europe’s vulnerability in critical minerals is overwhelmingly one of refining. According to the International Energy Agency’s 2025 Global Critical Minerals Outlook, China controls the processing of 19 out of 20 energy-transition minerals, with an average global market share above 70 per cent.
China weaponizes this dominant position by restricting the export of refined metals, refining technology, and equipment, and by adjusting prices to keep original equipment manufacturers (OEM) consuming and making life hard for competitors.
The EU’s import reliance for refined materials climbed from roughly 83 per cent in 2011 to 90 per cent by 2023, even as its raw ore imports stayed comparatively stable. That gap between mining exposure and refining exposure became impossible to ignore once it started costing European factories production days. Between 2023 and 2025, Chinese export controls on gallium, germanium, graphite and rare earth technologies produced real stoppages on European assembly lines.
Trafigura CEO Richard Holtum correctly pointed out that “Europe’s smelters are strategic assets we cannot afford to lose.” The good news — despite the erosion of the midstream due to high energy costs and subsidized Chinese overcapacity — is that Europe retains a significant industrial base of metals smelters and “with targeted investment, existing assets could be modernized and expanded”, per Holtum. For a relatively small sum compared to the cost of inaction, existing zinc smelters can produce germanium, while alumina smelters can produce gallium.
The EU CRMA 40 per cent figure sought to be ambitious without coming at the expense of processing expanding in developing countries. This value addition is something they insist on for economic and social development. Europe agrees and it is in Europe’s interest to help its partners to process materials close to the mine and then to ship value-added materials directly to the European market instead of sending concentrates for processing in China.
The EU’s strategy to achieve its 2030 CRMA benchmarks relies essentially on:
- prioritizing the materials most essential to strategic technologies of the future, such as clean tech, digital, defence and aerospace;
- selecting strategic projects that make a meaningful contribution toward the benchmarks – 28 out of the 60 strategic projects announced in 2025 were for refining (or integrated mining and refining);
- streamlining and speeding up the permitting of strategic projects without weakening environmental or social protections – 15 months from when the project promoter submits a complete application file to the relevant authority for refining and recycling projects, 27 months for mining projects;
- facilitating public and private finance, although the CRMA lacks a dedicated fund, existing programs are being repurposed and the December 2025 RESourceEU action plan mobilized C4.8 billion (€3 billion ) in EU‑level financing instruments to support CRMA strategic projects;
- strategic partnerships with countries outside the EU – there are currently 16 of these; and
- demand-side measures, including demand aggregation and joint purchasing as well as incentives for supply chain diversification in EU public procurement rules.
Where does implementation of the 40 per cent benchmark stand?
The benchmark points out the direction of travel, but it is not a legally binding number. By itself, setting a benchmark cannot override the economic fundamentals of Europe’s high energy, regulatory and labour costs, weak demand from downstream sectors, or much cheaper Chinese materials.
Progress differs sharply by material. On the credit side, lithium refining capacity has grown, anchored by AMG Lithium’s hydroxide plant in Germany. Nickel and cobalt chemicals production has strengthened through Umicore, Terrafame and new precursor plants in Poland. Greece’s vertically integrated aluminium producer Metlen is on track to produce gallium.
Rare-earth separation and magnet recycling, which barely existed in Europe five years ago, are taking early shape through Solvay, Carester and MagREEsource in France and Neo Performance Materials in Estonia, with feedstock due to come onstream in Sweden and Norway before long.
Against that, the debit side is substantial. Nearly a third of Europe’s base-metal smelting capacity has closed or been curtailed over the past decade, for the reasons explained above. Magnesium and titanium metal still have essentially no European refining base at all. Several silicon metal facilities are shuttered due to the inability to compete with China’s prices.
Canada, overreliant on the U.S. market, urgently needs to diversify, while EU companies need to become much more active as offtakers and investors to secure minerals and refined metals from Canada, the EU’s reliable and stable partner in North America.
Overall, the assessment now must be that while the EU is unlikely to achieve its 40 per cent refining benchmark by 2030, it is far better to try than to simply let this sector shrivel in the face of ruthless and rigged competition.
What should Canada and Europe take from this?
First, Canada has its own Critical Minerals Strategy (2022), positioning it to become a global mining and critical minerals leader, not just in what it extracts but in how it builds, processes and delivers value from the mine all the way to the market. That foundation is sound, but the shifts in global supply chains since 2022, and the midstream opportunities set out below, make a strong case for refreshing and sharpening the strategy.
Canada produces a broad suite of strategic minerals and maintains processing capacity in areas such as aluminum, nickel, copper, cobalt and zinc, alongside recovery of key by‑products like indium and tellurium. These capabilities are underpinned by access to reliable, low‑cost and low‑carbon electricity.
Second, Canada and the EU have a strong bilateral relationship. The Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) provides a preferential trade framework most competitors lack. The 2021 EU-Canada strategic partnership on critical raw materials anchors the bilateral partnerships with countries such as France and Germany as well as corporate deals backed politically by public authorities on both sides of the Atlantic.
Recognizing the growing importance of middle powers’ alignment, Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have nominated special envoys to drive the bilateral relationship forward — John Hannaford for Canada and Joost Korte for the Commission.
While the political framing is excellent, the strategic partnership on critical raw materials (CRM) needs more solid projects and co-investments. Canada, overreliant on the U.S. market, urgently needs to diversify, while EU companies need to become much more active as offtakers and investors to secure minerals and refined metals from Canada, the EU’s reliable and stable partner in North America.
Concretely, this means building a dynamic project pipeline, backed by joint financing for shared midstream plants, offtake agreements guaranteeing European buyers for Canadian-processed material, reciprocal fast-track permitting for jointly designated strategic projects, and pairing Canada’s low-carbon power with European separation and recycling know-how.
Third, during its G7 presidency in 2025, Canada announced the first round of the G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance: 26 new investments and partnerships with nine allied countries. Several of these were midstream facilities which would benefit from tighter European involvement: Rio Tinto’s scandium refining expansion in Sorel‑Tracy; Ucore’s Kingston rare‑earth refinery advanced samarium and gadolinium processing; Northern Graphite’s graphite processing tolling deal with Italy’s Alkeemia and Torngat Metals’ Strange Lake rare earths mine’s separation technology tie-up with France’s Ca

Original article: Vietnam y su plan para girar de exportador de tierras raras en bruto a refinador en suelo nacional
For years, Vietnam has navigated a challenging position in the geopolitics of critical minerals: it holds the second-largest rare earth reserves in the world but exports nearly all its crude ore, primarily to China. Now, Hanoi aims to change this narrative. The Ministry of Industry and Trade has finalized a draft decree that, if enacted, would prohibit the export of unprocessed rare earth ore and 16 other strategic minerals, requiring that any sale abroad meets strict deep processing thresholds in Vietnam. This draft, submitted to the Ministry of Justice for review on October 8, is not yet law. However, its existence signifies a seismic shift in Hanoi’s strategy: moving from a raw materials supplier to a significant player in the global value chain.
The Draft: 17 Minerals Under Lock
The document, titled “List of Strategic and Important Minerals Permitted for Export and their Processing Levels”, identifies 17 of the 19 minerals on Vietnam’s strategic list. It includes rare earths, tin, tungsten, antimony, copper, bauxite, titanium, lithium, iron, manganese, molybdenum, nickel, cobalt, chromite, anthracite coal, apatite, and graphite. Uranium, thorium, and gold are excluded from this specific regime.
The rule is simply formulated but radical in effect: only products that have reached the specified deep processing level for each mineral may be exported. Direct export of raw ore or concentrates is prohibited. For tin, for instance, refined metal is required, even in ingots. Tungsten must be processed into ammonium paratungstate (APT) or tungsten oxide. Copper is allowed only in refined cathodes or plates.
The case for rare earths is even more restrictive. They do not follow the general rule of the draft, which allows the export of any product that surpasses a processing threshold. Rare earths have a special management mechanism: they may only leave the country in one of five forms: individual rare earth oxides (separated), rare earth metals, alloys, alloy powders, or permanent magnets. Minerals, concentrates, and intermediate products are strictly prohibited.
No Transition, No New Procedures
Two details of the draft reveal the urgency with which Hanoi wants to implement this shift. First, there is no transition period. The criterion for determining if a shipment is governed by the new policy is the time of customs declaration. Contracts signed prior to the law’s enactment are not automatically protected. Second, the text does not create new administrative procedures, a concession to the exporting community that does not mitigate the impact of the fundamental prohibition.
The Gap Between Paper and Factory
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Vietnam possesses an estimated 22 million tons of rare earth oxides, roughly half of China’s reserves and more than any other country. Mining production has skyrocketed tenfold in recent years, increasing from 400 tons in 2021 to 4,300 tons by 2025, propelling Vietnam to the sixth-largest global producer, up from tenth place in 2021.
However, this explosive growth conceals a paradox that the draft seeks to rectify. Vietnam lacks a single operational industrial plant capable of refining ore into high-purity rare earth oxides (≥95%), the minimum standard for export and use in advanced technology. Current activities focus on extraction and primary processing. As Professor Tran Dai Lam from the Institute of Materials Science at the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology states: “A country that possesses rare earths but only extracts and exports them as primary ore or concentrates is selling the lowest part of the value chain.”
The primary beneficiary of this dynamic has been China. Chinese customs data shows that imports of rare earth elements and concentrates from Vietnam doubled to nearly 12,000 tons in the last recorded year. Vietnam also imported rare earths to process and re-export, an anomaly the new framework seeks to eliminate.
The Legal Framework is Already in Progress
The Ministry of Industry and Trade’s draft is supported by a broader legislative change: the Amended Law on Geology and Minerals, approved by the National Assembly on December 11, 2025, and effective from January 1, 2026. This law formally classifies rare earths as a special strategic resource under strict state supervision and prohibits the export of raw ore. The regulation stipulates that only designated or authorized entities by the Government can carry out exploration, extraction, and processing activities for rare earths, with the State centrally managing geological data.
The Ministry of Industry’s draft operationalizes this legal prohibition, defining what is meant by “deep processing” for each mineral and closing the regulatory loophole that previously allowed the export of concentrates.
The Global Industry is Already Moving
Despite the draft not yet being enacted, the international private sector is already positioning itself. In March 2026, Australian Lynas Rare Earths—the largest rare earth producer outside of China—signed a framework agreement with South Korean LS Eco Energy to build a rare earth metal production facility in Vietnam. The facility will convert rare earth oxides into metals, initially prioritizing samarium, and produce neodymium-praseodymium metals (NdPr) and heavy elements like dysprosium and terbium, critical inputs for permanent magnets in electric vehicles and wind turbines. Both companies signed convertible instruments worth approximately 30 million Australian dollars each as a signal of long-term commitment.
Simultaneously, Hanoi has activated a regulatory sandbox mechanism to test semi-industrial-scale refining technology. In September 2026, the Hanoi People’s Committee authorized the Construction Consulting and Mining Technology Joint Stock Company to execute a pilot project to produce total rare earth oxides with purity above 95% from ore sourced from Dong Pao mine in Lai Chau province. The plant is designed for a capacity of 100 kilograms of ore per hour and a maximum of 100 tons of processed ore, with an 18-month testing period. The project is financed 80% by the company’s own resources.
The Challenge: Technology, Not Ore
Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh himself has acknowledged that the central challenge is not a lack of resources but the absence of technological capacity to convert those resources into value. In a meeting of the Government’s Standing Committee in January 2026, Chinh emphasized the need to develop the rare earth industry to ensure national strategic autonomy, prioritizing deep processing, advanced technology transfer, public-private collaboration, and infrastructure development.
The official roadmap, however, is ambitious. The Government has planned to raise annual rare earth mineral production to 2 million tons by 2030, a goal that would multiply current production by more than 450 times. Achieving this would require not only massive investment in separation and refining plants but also the training of specialized human capital and resolution of regulatory bottlenecks that analysts believe still persist despite legislative advances.
What Is at Stake
If the draft is enacted without changes, Vietnam will cease to be a marginal supplier of concentrates and instead become a gatekeeper of its own subterranean resources. Countries that currently import Vietnamese raw ore—China primarily—will have to adapt: either purchase already processed products or establish refining capacity in Vietnam. For Western nations looking to diversify their rare earth supply chains away from China, Vietnam’s maneuver presents both an opportunity and a warning: Hanoi is not willing to be a mere raw material supplier in that strategy. It aims to be a partner and intends to retain the added value.
The draft is now in the hands of the Ministry of Justice. Its approval—or modification—will determine whether Vietnam successfully bridges the gap between the 22 million tons that lie beneath its soil and the magnets, alloys, and metals that the world requires.

In southeastern Colorado, the drought has decimated the corn crop. This season has been the worst Derek White Heckman, based in McClave, Colorado, has experienced since he began farming in 2018.
“It’s been dry for quite a while,” said White Heckman, a board member of the Colorado Corn Promotion Council. “We’ve been in a long-term drought.”
“If we had two or three years of this, it would be really tough on guys and you might see a lot more bankruptcies in the area,” White Heckman said. Looking back, he recalled severe drought in the early 2000s and 2011–2012, but said the current drought was worse than earlier droughts.
White Heckman grows corn, forage crops, and rotates in crops such as pinto beans and sunflowers, while also incorporating cattle into his operation. He’s learned to lean on crop diversification and soil health practices to manage through these dry times.
The latest U.S. Drought Monitor data, released Oct. 8, shows drought categories for Colorado as:
- 15.62% None
- 12.91% Abnormally Dry (D0)
- 16.28% Moderate Drought (D1)
- 22.25% Severe Drought (D2)
- 24.47% Extreme Drought (D3)
- 8.47% Exceptional Drought (D4)
While he has irrigation, the operation relies on a canal system supplied by the river rather than groundwater from wells. The area’s snow basin recorded its lowest snowpack on record, White Heckman explained.
“In a normal year, we usually get an average of 25 runs of water, and I think we’re on run six now,” White Heckman said.
Crop losses have been significant. White Heckman decided to switch about 95% of his corn acreage to silage. “We just didn’t think that there was going to be much,” he said. “It probably would have made under 50 bushels per acre (bpa), and we shoot for 200- to 250-bushel corn.”
“There was basically nothing there, but enough to run a chopper through and we maybe got two tons an acre on some of those fields,” said White Heckman.
Lessons Learned
“Soil health practices are making a difference,” White Heckman explained. “When we did get rainfall, I know we got it all. It’s allowing our crops to survive a little bit longer.”
Fields with more soil health practices appeared to produce better corn tonnage and withstand the drought a little bit better, he said.
“We’re very thankful for insurance,” White Heckman said. “You hate to use it, but in the times like this, it’s beneficial to make sure that you can still pay your operating note and hope for a better year next year.”
Weather
“Widespread heavy precipitation abetted robust improvement across eastern Colorado,” according to the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). “Numerous locations reported 3 inches to locally over 6 inches of rain, which was sufficient to support two-category improvements in portions of southeastern Colorado.”
“We have caught a lot of moisture, which has been a blessing,” White Heckman said of the recent rainfall. “Drought maps look better than they did, back in July.”
According to the USDM map, the only areas where conditions deteriorated were in northeastern Colorado.
“Historical correlation analysis shows El Niño is also linked to changes in Colorado weather, where conditions are generally wetter during El Niño years,” said Peter Goble, assistant state climatologist of Colorado for the Colorado Climate Center, in a Colorado State University climate blog article. “This is especially true in fall and spring, when much of the state averages higher precipitation. Furthermore, the Front Range and Eastern Plains are more prone to large spring snowstorms and experience fewer dry and windy spring days (though such days remain frequent regardless).”
“Unfortunately, the link between the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and peak seasonal snowpack levels in Colorado is weak,” Goble said. “Southern river basins, such as the San Juan and Rio Grande, show a loose positive correlation between El Niño and snowpack.”
Crop Progress
Corn
The Crop Production report, released Oct. 9, forecasts Colorado corn yields to decline in 2026 by 36 bpa from an average of 133 bpa in 2025 to 97 bpa in 2026. Colorado farmers are expected to harvest 113.49 million bushels of corn across 1.17 million acres this season, according to the report.
The USDA Crop Progress report, released Oct. 13, rated Colorado corn condition 15% very poor, 36% poor, 13% fair, 36% good, and 0% excellent.
Sorghum
The USDA rated Colorado sorghum condition 19% very poor, 25% poor, 20% fair, 36% good, and 0% excellent.

Glencore’s (LON: GLEN), (ASX: GLC) shares traded heavily in their debut on Wednesday on the Australian Securities Exchange, where the miner and trader hopes to secure a better valuation from investors seeking greater copper exposure.
Glencore CEO Gary Nagle expects strong demand from Australian investors betting on copper’s role in electrification, he said on Friday, as demand rises for the metal’s use in power grid expansions, transport and AI data centres.
“Glencore has been investing in Australia for decades and we know the Australian investment community has a sophisticated understanding of global resources and commodity markets,” Nagle said in a statement on Wednesday.
Glencore CHESS Depositary Interests (CDIs) closed at A$11.23 ($7.86), down 1.8% from their opening at A$11.44, with more than 4 million shares changing hands. Shares in its large mining rivals on the Australian market, BHP Group (ASX: BHP) and Rio Tinto (ASX: RIO), also fell.
Glencore shares already trade in London with another secondary listing in Johannesburg. On a pence equivalent, the CDIs opened at 603 pence and finished at 592.64 pence, a small premium to Glencore’s last close on the London Stock Exchange at 582.90.
Nagle has previously said he believes the $88 billion company can achieve inclusion in Australia’s benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index within 12 months, but analysts see momentum behind the stock potentially propelling it into the top indexes in half that time.
“It is not every day that a company of Glencore’s scale joins the ASX, particularly in a period of subdued listing activity,” said Paul Schroder, a partner at law firm Mallesons.
“Its arrival is a significant addition to the Australian market and reinforces the ASX’s standing as a leading resources exchange.”
Buyout opportunities
Analysts and investors speculated Glencore’s decision to list Down Under could help acclimatise those who had not seen value in its approach to Rio Tinto last year.
Rio Tinto walked away from takeover talks with Glencore in February, ending months of negotiations over a $240 billion tie-up that would have reshaped the global mining industry.
Nagle told reporters last week that a deeper local presence in Australia, where it produces coal, copper, zinc, lead and nickel, may yield business opportunities, although it had no set buyout list.
JPMorgan analysts said on Friday after a meeting with Nagle that Glencore’s management team still saw merits in a combination with Rio Tinto and noted its shares had outperformed its Anglo-Australian rival by 10% since negotiations collapsed in February.
“M&A is seen as part of the growth strategy and it was noted ‘who knows what happens in the future,'” the analysts said in a report.

Highlights
- Cheniere Energy is the largest American exporter of liquefied natural gas.
- Record export volumes and terminal expansion have kept the company in the spotlight.
- Long-term sale agreements underpin a large share of the company's export capacity.
Recent attention on Cheniere Energy has centered on its record pace of exports and its lifted production plans, with the company signaling it expects to ship a greater volume of liquefied natural gas than ever before. Management commentary has pointed to brisk demand from overseas buyers and to the ramp-up of newly built capacity at its terminals. That combination of record output and expanding infrastructure has kept the name among the most closely watched across the energy group.
What Cheniere Energy does
Cheniere Energy liquefies natural gas and exports it by sea to customers around the world. The company operates large coastal terminals where gas drawn from American pipelines is chilled to a liquid state, loaded onto specialized tankers and shipped overseas. At the destination, the fuel is warmed back into gas and fed into local networks. This process allows American gas, after confined largely to the domestic market, to reach buyers across oceans. The company runs its export business primarily through long sale agreements, in which buyers commit to take fixed volumes over many years and pay fees tied to the use of the terminals.
Record export volumes
The surge in export volumes has been the headline theme for the company. As newly built liquefaction capacity has come online and existing units have run hard, the amount of fuel shipped from its terminals has climbed to record levels. Management has indicated the company expects to reach volumes it has never previously achieved, a milestone that underscores the scale the business has reached since it pioneered large-scale American gas exports. Reaching record output reflects both the expansion of physical capacity and strong demand from buyers eager to secure American supply. Each incremental unit of liquefaction added at the terminals lifts the volume the company can ship, and the steady pull from overseas customers has kept that capacity busy.
Terminal expansion
Expansion of the company's terminals has been a continuing storyline, as new liquefaction units are built and brought into service to lift total capacity. These projects are large, multi-year undertakings that require substantial capital and careful construction, but they steadily widen the volume of gas the company can process and export. The appeal of the broader export business across US Energy Stocks has been closely tied to exactly this kind of capacity growth. Adding capacity positions the company to serve demand that is expected to grow as more buyers seek American gas. The expansion of its coastal facilities extends the physical base from which it operates and deepens its standing as the leading American exporter of the fuel. Readers following Energy Stocks can place this update within its wider category.
Long-term sale agreements
A defining feature of Cheniere Energy is the extent to which its capacity is committed under long sale agreements. Buyers from around the world sign contracts to take fixed volumes over many years, paying fees for the right to use the terminals regardless of how much fuel they ultimately lift. This arrangement gives the company a dependable base of fees and reduces its exposure to short-term swings in the price of gas. These agreements also provide the financial foundation for the company's expansion. Lenders and the firm itself can plan large terminal projects with greater confidence when a substantial share of the new capacity is already committed to buyers.
The global gas trade
Buyers in Europe have turned to American fuel to diversify their supply, while importers across Asia have drawn on it to meet growing demand. Cheniere Energy, as the pioneer of large-scale American exports, has been central to that transformation. The trade is shaped by a web of factors, from the pace of demand growth in importing regions to the construction of new export capacity around the world. Competition comes from exporters in other producing nations, and the balance between global supply and demand influences prices and contracting activity. Within that landscape, the company's scale, its established terminals and its deep contract base have given it a prominent place in the market.

Codelco

Conversations about artificial intelligence and copper typically start with the extra tonnage that data centers will need, yet that lens misses a possibly bigger transformation. In an op-ed carried by Mining.com, AI is described as ushering in a fresh category of copper purchaser with an exceptionally strong readiness to pay, and as such buyers claim a larger portion of incremental demand in a market where supply is tight, they may gain growing sway over prices and alter which users consume the metal, the purposes it serves and the direction the market takes.
Although it is digital in nature, AI relies on a considerable physical base encompassing data centers, transformers, substations, cooling systems, new electricity generation and transmission lines. The International Energy Agency forecasts that worldwide data center electricity use will climb from roughly 415 TWh in 2024 to approximately 945 TWh by 2030, more than doubling across six years. Industry estimates referenced in the op-ed indicate that data centers might need about 30 tonnes of copper for every megawatt of installed capacity, subject to design and the infrastructure involved, before counting the broader power networks required to supply them.
AI is not emerging on its own. It overlaps with electrification, the energy transition and a geopolitical drive to restore domestic manufacturing, diversify supply chains and enlarge military capacity. These forces have distinct rationales, yet each calls for heavy spending on physical assets before economic returns appear, signaling an exceptionally material-intensive period of global investment.
Such demand encounters an industry that has difficulty expanding. Falling grades, deeper deposits, more complicated ores, water limitations and drawn-out permitting have rendered new supply slower and costlier. Moving a new mine from discovery to production can now require well over 15 years. Chile, the largest copper producer worldwide, has found it hard to grow output despite its enormous resource base and sizable investment pipeline. Throughout the sector, maintaining output at mature operations increasingly demands major capital outlays, while opening new deposits brings mounting technical, environmental and regulatory hurdles.
When supply adjusts slowly, even fairly small demand increases can produce notable market consequences. As the expense of developing new production grows and high-value technological uses multiply, the two together could underpin structurally higher copper prices without removing the cycles that are intrinsic to commodity markets.
Inside an AI data center, where total investment can surpass $30 million per megawatt, copper might make up only about 1% of the overall cost, depending on the facility's configuration and the infrastructure involved. For hyperscalers competing to roll out computing capacity, obtaining infrastructure on schedule counts for far more than swings in the price of the metal within it.
Conventional copper consumers confront a different situation. Producers of cables, construction products, appliances and electrical equipment tend to be more exposed to raw material expenses, though how sensitive they are hinges on their capacity to pass those costs along to buyers and on whether substitutes exist. Since both groups operate in the same global market, their divergent willingness to pay is significant. As high-value technological uses make up a rising share of incremental demand, that willingness to pay could increasingly determine the marginal price of copper, squeezing traditional users that have less room to absorb higher costs.
The outcome need not be reduced aggregate demand, but rather a change in its makeup, with quicker gains in material efficiency, product redesign, recycling and substitution, especially by aluminum where technically and economically viable. For forecasters, aggregate consumption projections alone no longer suffice; grasping who can pay, and who will look for alternatives, is becoming as crucial as gauging how much copper the world will use.
A second, longer-range uncertainty involves the link between AI-driven productivity and material consumption. AI holds out the promise of efficiency gains throughout the economy, from engineering design to logistics and resource allocation, possibly lowering the materials needed per unit of output. History, though, urges prudence. In 1865, William Stanley Jevons noted that more efficient steam engines had not cut Britain's coal consumption but had instead helped it grow, as cheaper energy spurred new uses. With copper, gains in material efficiency have not stopped global consumption from rising as electrification, industrialization and new applications have proliferated.
Better efficiency does not automatically translate into lower aggregate consumption. By cutting costs and opening new economic possibilities, AI could spur further investment, electricity demand and infrastructure development. How these forces will play out over time remains the question. This uncertainty argues against both extending today's demand growth without limit and presuming that technological efficiency will inevitably curb future copper consumption.
Most focus has fallen on the copper AI will use, and less on the copper it could help extract. Machine learning can sharpen exploration targeting; advanced analytics can refine mine plans and equipment utilization; AI-based process control can boost grinding efficiency and flotation performance. The gains can be substantial. At a mine yielding 300,000 tonnes of copper each year with an 85% metallurgical recovery rate, lifting recovery by a single percentage point would add roughly 3,500 tonnes annually, potentially with modest additional capital investment.
Reaping these benefits takes more than purchasing software. It calls for dependable data, integrated systems, skilled personnel and organizations capable of acting on what the models show. The true measure of AI in mining will not be how many pilots are announced, but how much extra copper is produced and how much costs are lowered.
AI will probably reinforce copper demand, yet its most enduring impact may fall on the market's structure. Some consumers may manage to absorb considerably higher prices, while others confront mounting incentives to replace copper. Meanwhile, technological innovation is altering the economics of producing the metal itself. In such a market, elevated prices can also speed up the efficiency gains and substitution that undercut copper's traditional markets.
Firms that seize this window to lift productivity and develop technological capabilities will be better positioned to endure future cycles. The same holds for producing nations, whose opportunity goes beyond shipping more metal to cultivating technologies, engineering capabilities and mining services that can compete on a global scale. The task is to grasp a demand whose composition is shifting and to deploy AI itself to build a more productive mining industry. Copper's future will hinge not only on how much the world requires, but on who can afford it and how effectively the industry can supply it.
The op-ed was authored by Juan Carlos Guajardo, executive director of Chile-based consultancy Plusmining.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina and SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Giraffe Bio, a company developing programmable biomolecules to recover critical minerals with a lower environmental footprint, has raised a $6.4 million Seed round to validate and scale its mineral-specific reagent platform.

Copper is essential to power grids, renewable energy, electric vehicles and data infrastructure, but meeting rising demand will require miners to recover more metal from lower-grade and more complex ores.
Concurrently, flotation, the process used to separate valuable minerals from unwanted material, underpins roughly 80% of global copper production and plays a critical role in determining the quality and quantity of copper a mine can recover.
Yet much of the chemistry used in floatation was developed decades ago.
Giraffe Bio is applying a drug-discovery playbook to mining, combining AI-enabled molecular design, cell-free biology and testing on real ore samples to engineer biochemical promoters for copper flotation. Tailored to specific minerals and ore conditions, these reagents are designed to help mines recover more copper and other valuable minerals while producing cleaner concentrates.
These finished, drop-in reagents work alongside existing flotation chemicals, without requiring new equipment or infrastructure. They bring the precision of molecular design to mineral processing without relying on living organisms in the mining operation.

EnergyX Signs $2-Billion Lithium Offtake Agreement with Trafigura
EnergyX has entered into a binding offtake arrangement worth $2-billion to provide commodities trader Trafigura with lithium from Chile and the United States, according to Mining Weekly. The transaction, characterized as among the biggest ever linked to direct lithium extraction technology, spans a decade.
Through the take-or-pay contract, Trafigura will acquire 100 000 metric tons of lithium from EnergyX across the 10-year term. The agreement's worth is pegged to prevailing lithium prices around $20 000 per metric ton.
Trafigura will purchase 5 000 metric tons annually of lithium hydroxide and an equivalent yearly quantity of lithium carbonate from EnergyX. Battery producers generally prefer one variant over the other based on the device the battery is meant to power.
Daniel von Arx, who leads battery metals at Trafigura, stated that the arrangement demonstrates the company's capacity to assist in bringing strategic critical minerals projects into operation and to establish secure, diversified supply chains.
EnergyX, established in 2018 and supported by General Motors and Italian energy firm Eni, intends to commence lithium production in 2028. The company plans to initially generate 15 000 metric tons per year of lithium hydroxide in Texas beginning in 2029, with Trafigura taking 33% of that volume. In Chile, EnergyX aims to begin producing 7 500 metric tons per year of lithium carbonate in 2028, with Trafigura's portion accounting for 66% of output in that nation.
Switzerland-headquartered Trafigura intends to initially sell the lithium to Chinese buyers, with a longer-term ambition of becoming a major supplier to US markets once that country's battery supply chain matures.
EnergyX is among the firms pursuing direct lithium extraction, a broad category of filtration technology akin to household water softeners. Exxon Mobil, Vulcan Energy Resources and Lilac Solutions are among the others advancing DLE. While some are creating their own DLE systems, EnergyX has merged several established filtration technologies and constructed them using readily obtainable equipment, an approach that drew Trafigura's interest.
EnergyX has been trialing its processes at its Austin, Texas laboratory. It requires additional funding to construct the Chile and Texas facilities. The deal assists in progressing EnergyX's application with the US Export-Import Bank for a $690-million loan.
Although privately held EnergyX has previously discussed a potential public listing, CEO and founder Teague Egan said his current focus is on supplying lithium to the company's first customer. Egan said EnergyX must build and begin producing commercial lithium before it can even contemplate a public offering.
When questioned about recent lithium market volatility, Egan said he anticipates demand will keep climbing and could surpass supply in the years ahead, calling the fundamentals strong and observing that total global demand rises consistently year after year.
Beyond lithium, Egan said EnergyX intends to move into the uranium sector, with plans to mine and enrich the nuclear fuel. He said the demand curve for uranium today resembles what lithium experienced a decade ago.
Trafigura also holds a lithium offtake with Standard Lithium, which is developing an Arkansas DLE project. Trafigura competitor Glencore has concluded lithium deals with DLE developer Eramet and recycling startup Nth Cycle, among others.
The agreement arrives as robust demand for lithium from the rapidly expanding stationary battery storage system market has counterbalanced inconsistent sales in the global electric vehicle market, which had been the metal's main consumer for years.
