articles.title: What Happened to Pennsylvania’s Hydrogen Hubs? - Inside Climate News
articles.summary: What Happened to Pennsylvania’s Hydrogen Hubs?  Inside Climate News
articles.full_text:
Three years ago, hydrogen seemed poised for a long-awaited breakthrough. The Biden administration announced $7 billion in federal funding for seven hubs to produce the fuel across the country, and Pennsylvania was set to be a major player in the emerging industry.
Hydrogen has long been heralded as a potential skeleton key to emission reductions: able to power commuter vehicles and mass transportation, as well as hard-to-decarbonize industries like shipping and steel production.
During a 2023 speech at Philadelphia’s Tioga Terminal, President Joe Biden assured the crowd that Pennsylvania’s two hubs—the Mid Atlantic Regional Hydrogen Hub and the Appalachian Hydrogen Hub, commonly known as MACH2 and ARCH2—would be transformational. The hubs would connect a vast network of hydrogen producers, users, and researchers across Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, West Virginia and Ohio. They were backed by a bipartisan coalition and designed to bring economic opportunity to red states, with support in Pennsylvania from both Gov. Josh Shapiro and Sen. Dave McCormick. In 2023, Shapiro said the hubs would “ensure Pennsylvania continues to be an energy leader for decades to come.”
MACH2 promised to bring over 20,000 jobs to the Delaware Valley region alone and lead the way in green hydrogen, produced entirely from clean energy, with a $750 million award from the Department of Energy. ARCH2 would receive $925 million to manufacture blue hydrogen, produced via fossil fuels, with emissions sequestered by carbon capture technology. ARCH2 would be centered on Western Pennsylvania’s steel industry.
Today, that momentum has all but disappeared, one of many clean energy investments facing an uncertain future under the Trump administration. ARCH2 has gone totally dark, with former partners denying involvement or stonewalling media requests, and MACH2 has entered a holding pattern. Experts with knowledge of the hubs say that the federal government has been playing a game of “will they, won’t they”—changing their minds from week to week.
Community groups who initially opposed the hubs say they’ve heard nothing about the projects for months, although Manny Cintron, CEO of MACH2, told Inside Climate News via email that the hub’s “award is active,” but partners “continue to proceed cautiously in light of the current budget uncertainty.” In other words, no one wants to move forward with investment until they have a sense of whether the federal government will continue to fund the hub. As of late September, MACH2 was still circulating a request from January for potential partners to join the hub. The Department of Energy did not respond to repeated requests for comment.
“Until I see significant evidence to the contrary, I just don’t think the hubs are happening,” said Tom Torres, chief of staff at the Ohio River Valley Institute, a think tank focused on Appalachia.
This outcome is exactly what the hydrogen industry feared in the wake of the 2024 election. Losing the funding is going to “harm Pennsylvania,” Shapiro told Axios last year. “It’s going to mean we’re producing less energy. I have no idea why the president of the United States would want to do that.”
Even before Donald Trump took office, the hubs were facing an uphill battle, held up by a long lobbying fight over who would qualify for the 45V tax credits, which offered producers up to $3 per kilogram of hydrogen produced. Oil and gas proponents wanted more carve-outs for blue hydrogen hubs, like ARCH2; environmentalists wanted to ensure that the subsidies went to hubs running solely off of clean energy, rather than pulling from Pennsylvania’s gas-heavy grid. The debate dragged on nearly until Biden left office, delaying investment and leaving the projects in limbo.
To complicate matters, green hydrogen, which involves using clean energy to produce a different kind of clean energy, is notoriously difficult to produce cost effectively. The fuel is created through a process called electrolysis—essentially, running an electrical current through water, which separates the hydrogen and the oxygen. If you hook a solar panel up to an electrolyzer, about 30 percent of the energy from that panel will be lost just in the process of isolating the hydrogen. By the time you compress it into a fuel cell or liquefy it for transport, then convert it back into electricity, about 70 percent of the energy generated by that original solar panel is gone. And even once you’ve managed to produce it, hydrogen is exceedingly leaky—the smallest element in the periodic table, able to escape even from sealed steel vats.
This is part of why the hubs drew so much pushback from environmental groups, who decried the fuel as a false solution when Biden’s plans were first announced. The United States currently produces about 10 million metric tons of hydrogen per year, almost all of which are made using oil and gas. Clean hydrogen is significantly more expensive, and even with subsidies, experts have warned that it will never be a practical or cost-competitive fuel for public transit, personal vehicles or commercial and residential heating.
But it is critical when it comes to replacing carbon-intensive chemical feedstocks that create products like ammonia, which is used to make fertilizer. Ammonia production alone accounts for roughly 2 percent of global energy consumption and 1.5 percent of greenhouse gas emissions. Green ammonia could also aid in decarbonizing global shipping, which produces another 3 percent of global emissions.
Under the Biden Administration, MACH-2 made a show of partnering with SEPTA, Philadelphia’s public transit system, to test hydrogen-powered buses. In the hub’s application, though, it was made clear that the main offtakers for MACH2 would, at least initially, be area oil refineries—a tough sell for community and environmental justice groups, who were already concerned about hydrogen’s high flammability and its potential to serve as an indirect greenhouse gas, magnifying the effects of methane, ozone and water vapor.
The second Trump administration gutted the Inflation Reduction Act, which invested billions in clean energy and incentives, but most of the hydrogen hubs were spared, at least on paper. Two hubs slated for California and the Pacific Northwest lost funding early on and remain mired in a legal battle, but the generous 45V hydrogen tax credit survived, albeit on a truncated timeline. Although it was initially reported that MACH2 was on the chopping block, Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced that the hydrogen hubs would retain their funding in April—but to what end is entirely unclear.
“What matters in the US more than hub status is whether individual projects are going ahead,” Martin Tengler, head of hydrogen research at BloombergNEF, told Inside Climate News in an email. Producers need to both find customers for their hydrogen and meet the deadlines to claim the 45V green hydrogen tax credit and the 45Q carbon capture credit, in the case of blue hydrogen hubs. “All these have been a challenge, except 45Q,” said Tengler.
Producers now have until December 31, 2027 to begin work before the tax credits expire, rather than the original deadline of 2032. That deadline seems all but impossible to meet, especially given the fact that the DOE does not plan to spend any more on the hubs this year, according to their July apportionment plan. ARCH2 could choose to take advantage of the 45Q tax credits for carbon capture, which don’t expire until 2033, but like MACH2, they’ve only drawn about one fifth of their total Phase One award money, “a drop in the bucket of the overall award,” said Torres.

Despite their funding reprieve, it’s not clear that the hubs will be able to hold on to that money over the next few years. The 2027 President’s Budget Request released in April currently calls for “permanently cancelling” unobligated funding for clean hydrogen programs and repurposing “Green New Scam funding” in favor of baseload power upgrades and spending $1.2 billion on the construction of seven AI supercomputers at Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories.
As a green hydrogen hub, MACH2 was dependent on the development of solar and offshore wind in order to operate. Although some solar projects are still moving forward, the American offshore wind industry has been effectively kneecapped over the last two years by the Trump administration.
Atlantic Shores Offshore Wind and Invenergy backed out of their contracts in 2025 amid delays and regulatory uncertainty, and early-stage products were abandoned after the Trump administration began paying companies out of their leases. In April, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities announced that they would no longer be building infrastructure to connect offshore wind to the grid. As a blue hydrogen hub, ARCH2 existed largely as a way for oil and gas to continue operating under stricter emissions regulations—somewhat redundant now that the Trump administration has moved to scrap emissions regulations for power plants entirely.
This was always part of the problem with the Biden administration’s initial plans, said Anika Juhn, an energy data analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Even if the government is willing to temporarily subsidize the production of clean hydrogen, that support won’t be enough unless there are complementary incentives on the demand side.
“The hydrogen story is really an ammonia story, in the U.S. at least,” said Juhn. articles.full_text:
- US commercial copper holdings are estimated at 1.1 million metric tons; reexports could increase supply elsewhere and reduce regional price premiums.
- A narrower US copper price premium could reduce imports for stockpiling if the price gap no longer covers shipping and financing costs, leaving more metal available elsewhere.
- Global copper mine output fell approximately 1% year over year in January-July 2026; releasing stored metal can improve availability but does not add new mine production.
- Power terms help developers estimate electricity costs, while resource estimates and recovery testing help explorers assess potential copper output.
- Inventory-related share-price declines could lower entry costs, but project selection still requires published cost estimates, tests of economics at lower copper prices, and funding covering the next milestone.
Tariff Expectations Concentrate Copper Stocks in the US
US commercial copper holdings total an estimated 1.1 million metric tons, including stocks outside exchange totals, according to Citi’s estimate cited in Reuters’ October 12, 2026 report. Commercial ownership means any release of this metal depends on the returns available from storage, domestic sales, or reexports.
The Commodity Exchange, Inc. (COMEX) warehouse report dated October 9, 2026 recorded approximately 713,347 metric tons of copper as of October 8. Exchange stocks overlap with the broader US estimate, so the totals should not be added. Registration for exchange delivery does not establish an owner’s intention to sell the metal for industrial use.
Declining Copper Mine Output Raises the Need for New Production
Redistributing stored copper can improve near-term availability, but it does not add mine production. Long-term project valuations must therefore assess copper price assumptions against future demand and mine supply, rather than warehouse stocks alone.
The International Copper Study Group (ICSG) reported preliminary year-over-year changes for January-July 2026, with mine production down approximately 1%, refined production up 1.7%, and apparent refined usage up 2.4%. Refined production includes recycled copper, so it can increase while mine output declines. Stored refined metal can meet some near-term demand, while additional mine capacity helps replace output lost elsewhere.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), in its Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, projects that base-case supply from existing and announced mines would fall approximately 25% short of 2035 copper requirements under its Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS). Those requirements deduct secondary supply, including recycled copper, from total demand and account for refining losses. Under these assumptions, narrowing the gap requires additional mine output, while resource studies, engineering, permits, and financing determine which projects can deliver that production.
Copper Price Uncertainty Makes Project Costs Central to Valuation
If inventory shifts lower copper prices, operating cost estimates help test whether projected revenue would cover production expenses. Engineering, permitting, and funding plans establish the work and capital required before production can begin.
Power Cost Estimates Support Disciplined Copper Project Financing
Power supply terms help estimate electricity expenses, while grid access and detailed engineering help define construction requirements.
Marimaca Copper secured grid connection approval and signed a preliminary Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) framework for its Marimaca Oxide Deposit (MOD), providing greater visibility over electricity supply and costs. Estimated power costs align closely with the Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) assumption of US$93 per megawatt-hour (MWh). Proposed ramp-up terms offer flexibility as operations start, while road upgrades and detailed engineering advance construction readiness.
Rising Mining Costs Require Testing Copper Project Returns
Economic studies assess whether recoverable copper can generate returns after construction and operating costs. Net Present Value (NPV) measures discounted project cash flow, while Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero. For expansions at existing mines, known as brownfield projects, declining grades and greater depth can increase the volume of rock processed and the work required to extract it.
Fitzroy Minerals reported approximately C$1.95 million in proceeds from early warrant exercises on October 8, 2026, adding funding for its Chilean copper work programs. Buen Retiro’s maiden Mineral Resource Estimate (MRE), Preliminary Economic Assessment (PEA), and environmental permit application are targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a Pre-Feasibility Study (PFS) in the second quarter of 2027. These studies aim to quantify recoverable copper, project economics, and development requirements for the proposed heap-leach operation.
Merlin Marr-Johnson, President and Chief Executive Officer of Fitzroy Minerals, explains why maintaining copper production requires increasing investment:
“Production growth within Chile, and in fact globally, is difficult. […] Brownfield has got more and more expensive, and that is a function of increased complexity, increased volumes as grades decline and increased depths as the big projects are being mined deeper and deeper and deeper.”
Projected Copper Supply Gaps Raise the Value of Resource Definition
Closer drilling and geological modeling can strengthen confidence in a deposit’s estimated copper content, while recovery testing helps assess how much copper could be recovered during processing. These inputs support estimates of potential production and revenue under different copper price assumptions.
Copper Supply Needs Support Plans to Restart Concentrate Production
Higher-confidence resources help define mineable areas, while processing tests assess recoverable output. Evaluating existing infrastructure helps establish its capacity and the refurbishment spending required for a restart.
Selkirk Copper completed 52,485 meters of Phase 2 drilling at Minto by September 28, exceeding its original 50,000-meter target. The results support resource conversion and mine-plan refinement, while samples will support planned copper, gold, and silver recovery testing for the upcoming feasibility study. Its completed PEA also informs management’s assessment of potential concentrate production.
M. Colin Joudrie, President and Chief Executive Officer of Selkirk Copper, explains how the restart strategy combines existing infrastructure with further technical work:
“It’s a solid study that reflects not just the asset itself, but that sort of accelerated timeline because it’s a restart. We’re not building from the ground up. […] We’re focusing on the mine plans and that integrated start.”
Copper Supply Needs Support Drilling to Establish Deposit Scale
Abitibi Metals Corp reported a drilled interval of 60.2 meters at 1.08% copper at B26, including 9.2 meters at 3.42% copper, supporting continuity within the deposit. Up to three drill rigs are planned for the remainder of 2026 to expand and better define the resource. The program is targeting resource expansion and conversion for a future resource update.
Cobra Resources reported a drilled interval of 23 meters at 0.63% copper at Blue Rose within its Manna Hill project in South Australia, including 12.4 meters at 1.01% copper. Mineralized intervals extend beyond 300 meters downhole and remain open, supporting further testing of the system’s dimensions. Follow-up drilling of up to 6,000 meters across 52 holes and four prospects has begun to test extensions and establish scale.
Mogotes Metals plans up to 20,000 meters of Filo Sur drilling in 2026-2027, targeting expansion of discoveries and a November 2026 restart subject to weather and access. At Beskauga, drilling has begun under a program of up to 50,000 meters, targeting initial results in the fourth quarter of 2026 and a PEA within 12 months of the September 22, 2026 announcement. The programs combine testing of deposit scale with planned economic evaluation.
Copper Trade Flows Test Whether Inventory Shifts Increase Overseas Supply
Slower US stockbuilding could reduce import demand even while inventories rise. Declining reported warehouse stocks show that withdrawals exceeded additions, but do not identify the metal’s destination.
US trade volumes and warehouse locations help distinguish reexports from domestic transfers, while the COMEX-LME price gap indicates whether US-bound shipments remain commercially attractive. Changes in exchange-delivery status alone do not confirm physical movement, so inventory releases must be assessed alongside trade and consumption data.
The Investment Thesis for Copper
- Inventory-related mining share-price declines could lower entry costs, with project value assessed using resource and recovery evidence for explorers and economic studies for more advanced projects.
- Power arrangements and infrastructure plans help quantify developers’ operating and construction costs, while permitting milestones help assess when production could begin.
- Converting resources into higher-confidence categories supports mine planning, while continuity and recovery testing help explorers assess deposit size and potential copper output.
- Economic studies should quantify recoverable copper and construction spending, with NPV and IRR sensitivities showing how project value and returns respond to different copper prices, recovery rates, and operating costs.
- Funding that covers spending through the next milestone helps sustain planned work during copper price declines, while permit status, infrastructure access, and local operating costs help assess development budgets and schedules.

(EnergyX) has signed a binding 10-year lithium offtake agreement with global commodity trader Trafigura, securing a long-term buyer for 100,000 metric tons of battery-grade lithium products and strengthening its plans to enter commercial production. Based on current indicative lithium prices of approximately $20,000 per metric ton, the agreement represents potential revenue exceeding $2 billion over its term, marking a significant commercial milestone for the company.
	Founded in 2018 by Teague Egan, EnergyX develops technologies for lithium extraction, refining, and critical mineral supply chains. The newly announced agreement is the company's first publicly disclosed lithium offtake contract and covers products from two flagship projects in the United States and Chile. Lithium carbonate will be supplied from the Black Giant™ project in Chile, while lithium hydroxide will come from Project Lonestar™ in Texas. A significant share of the contracted material is expected to support the US battery supply chain.
	The agreement provides EnergyX with greater commercial visibility as it advances its lithium production projects. Long-term offtake commitments can help emerging producers demonstrate market demand, strengthen financing discussions, and improve their ability to secure capital for large-scale construction. However, the potential revenue estimate is based on current indicative market prices and should not be interpreted as a guaranteed contract value, since actual prices and revenues will depend on the agreement's pricing terms and prevailing market conditions.
	EnergyX's commercial expansion is supported by its proprietary GET-Lit™ direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology platform, which the company says is protected by more than 150 patents. The technology is designed to extract lithium from brine resources and process it into battery-grade products. EnergyX commissioned Project Lonestar™ in Texas in April 2026, describing it as the largest DLE lithium production plant in the United States.
	The company is also advancing Project Black Giant™ in Chile, which is planned to have production capacity of 52,500 metric tons per year. 	EnergyX is continuing discussions with potential offtake partners across the battery, automotive, and energy storage sectors. The latest agreement strengthens its commercial position, while the pace of future production will depend on project execution, financing, and the successful expansion of its extraction and refining technology.
	Product and chemical commodity price impact
EnergyX's agreement with Trafigura strengthens the commercial outlook for battery-grade lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide by securing a long-term sales channel for planned production from Chile and Texas. The deal could improve financing prospects and encourage further investment in lithium extraction and refining capacity. However, additional production may eventually increase supply and limit price gains if capacity expands faster than demand. For ChemAnalyst-tracked commodities, the most direct implications concern lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide prices, while indirect effects may extend to battery materials and related chemicals. The contract alone is unlikely to trigger an immediate price increase; market balance remains decisive.

Japan's largest electricity producer Jera has made an investment of an undisclosed amount into US-based natural hydrogen explorer Koloma, according to the Japanese firm today (Thursday).
Through the investment, along with insight into Koloma’s natural hydrogen operations, Jera will “deepen its understanding of natural hydrogen’s potential as a future source of low-carbon energy”, though it is not clear exactly how Koloma will spend the money.
Koloma, which is headquartered in Denver, Colorado, has received investments of more than $400m in recent years, including those from Amazon and Bill Gates' climate investment vehicle Breakthrough Energy.
It also carries out acoustic surveys, and measures the Earth’s electromagnetic signals.
The firm is secretive about its operations but has been drilling for hydrogen in the US Midwest, as well as in other areas globally.
In July this year Koloma received exclusive rights from the Philippines government for natural hydrogen exploration in the Zambales Province, building on two service contracts it received in October last year for exploration in another area of the country.
It has also pursued operations in Australia, having in February last year revealed plans to launch a subsidiary in this country.
“Through investments in emerging technologies and businesses, Jera is exploring new energy solutions that can contribute to both energy security and decarbonisation,” Jera said today.

Oct 12 (Reuters) – Lithium startup EnergyX said on Monday it has signed a $2 billion binding offtake to supply commodities trader Trafigura with the battery metal from Chile and the US, one of the largest deals ever tied to direct lithium extraction technology.
The 10-year agreement, which Reuters is first to report, comes as strong demand for lithium from the fast-growing stationary battery storage system market has offset uneven sales in the global electric vehicle market, which had been the primary user of the ultralight metal for years.
Trafigura has agreed to buy 100,000 metric tons of lithium from EnergyX over a 10-year period as part of a take-or-pay contract. The deal’s value is tied to current lithium prices near $20,000 per metric ton.
“This agreement reflects our ability to help bring strategic critical minerals projects online and build secure, diversified supply chains,” said Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals.
As part of the agreement, Trafigura will buy 5,000 metric tons per year of lithium hydroxide and the same amount of lithium carbonate from EnergyX. Battery manufacturers typically prefer one version over the other, depending on what device the battery is powering.
EnergyX, which was formed in 2018 and is backed by General Motors and Italian energy company Eni, aims to start lithium production in 2028.
TRAFIGURA TARGETS US MARKET LONG TERM
The company plans to initially produce 15,000 metric tons per year of lithium hydroxide in Texas starting in 2029, meaning that Trafigura will buy 33% of that output.
In Chile, EnergyX plans to start producing 7,500 metric tons per year of lithium carbonate in 2028, with Trafigura’s share reflecting 66% of the output in the South American nation.
Switzerland-based Trafigura plans to initially sell the lithium to Chinese customers, with the long-term goal of being a large supplier to US markets once the country’s battery supply chain is developed.
EnergyX is among the companies pursuing direct lithium extraction (DLE), a broad classification of filtration technology comparable to household water softeners. Exxon Mobil, Vulcan Energy Resources and Lilac Solutions are among the others pursuing DLE.
While some are developing their own DLE systems, EnergyX has combined several known filtration technologies and built them with readily available equipment, a strategy that attracted Trafigura.
EnergyX has been testing its processes at its lab in Austin, Texas. It needs to obtain additional funds to build the Chile and Texas facilities.
The deal helps advance EnergyX’s application with the US Export-Import Bank for a $690 million loan.
While privately held EnergyX has discussed a possible public listing in the past, CEO and company founder Teague Egan said he is now focused on supplying lithium to his first customer.
“We need to build and start producing commercial lithium in order to even think about having a public offering,” said Egan.
When asked about the recent lithium market volatility, Egan said he expects demand to continue to rise and potentially outstrip supply in coming years.
“The fundamentals are strong,” Egan said. “Year in and year out, the total global demand continues to rise.”
Beyond lithium, Egan said EnergyX aims to expand into the uranium sector, with plans to mine and enrich the nuclear fuel.
“We see the demand curve for uranium today similar to what lithium was 10 years ago,” he said.
Trafigura also has a lithium offtake with Standard Lithium, which is developing an Arkansas DLE project.
Trafigura rival Glencore has inked lithium deals with DLE developer Eramet and recycling startup Nth Cycle, among others.

articles.title: PLS Group greenlights $1.3 billion expansion to lift Pilgangoora lithium output - Mining.com
articles.summary: PLS Group greenlights $1.3 billion expansion to lift Pilgangoora lithium output  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Australia’s PLS Group (ASX: PLS) has approved a final investment decision for its A$1.9 billion ($1.31 billion) project at its hard rock lithium mine Pilgangoora operation, betting on long-term growth in demand for the key battery-making ingredient.
The country’s largest independent lithium producer said the P2000 project will boost spodumene concentrate production at its flagship project in Western Australia to nearly 2 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) from 2029, through the construction of a new Jimmagunya processing plant.
Its shares rose more than 6% in early trading, set for their best day since August 24.
Energy transition and growth in battery storage continue to support the long-term demand for lithium, with companies worldwide racing to secure the metal.
PLS, formerly known as Pilbara, said the project was made possible by advances in processing technology that allowed around 67 million tonnes of material previously classified as waste to be brought into the mine plan, helping increase Pilgangoora’s ore reserve by 23% and contained lithium by 31%.
The project, it said, would lift average annual production to about 1.97 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate over the first 10 years of steady-state operations, while lowering average unit operating costs to around A$620 per tonne.
CEO Dale Henderson said the project would strengthen Pilgangoora’s position on the global lithium cost curve and provide greater exposure to any recovery in lithium prices.
The company also plans to invest a further A$600 million to A$650 million in supporting infrastructure, including a new accommodation village, road upgrades and maintenance facilities, while funding the development from its A$2.3 billion cash balance and operating cash flows.
PLS revised its FY27 capital expenditure forecast to be between A$1.11 billion and A$1.18 billion to incorporate the P2000 expansion and associated infrastructure spending.
It said the P2000 expansion would also produce tantalum, a critical mineral used in electronics and defence, as by-product.

articles.title: Don’t Stop ’Til You Get Enough – Are We Building Enough Gas Pipeline Capacity East Out of Katy? - RBN Energy
articles.summary: Don’t Stop ’Til You Get Enough – Are We Building Enough Gas Pipeline Capacity East Out of Katy?  RBN Energy
articles.full_text:
The volumes of Permian natural gas flowing into the Katy area west of Houston will be increasing sharply over the next few years, as will gas demand from new and expanding LNG export terminals near the Texas/Louisiana border. Three new pipelines with a combined capacity of 8 Bcf/d — Blackfin, Trident and Mustang Express — are being developed to move gas from Katy to the state line, but will that be enough? In today’s blog, we’ll use RBN’s Arrow Model to assess Enbridge’s recently unveiled proposal to add up to 2 Bcf/d of incremental capacity from Katy to the Gillis Hub in southwestern Louisiana.
We have blogged extensively over the past few years about three critically important and intertwined topics: fast-rising production of associated gas in the Permian, the massive buildout of new LNG export capacity along the Gulf Coast, and the frenetic development of gas pipeline capacity from Permian wells to water. Much of the discussion has focused on takeaway pipelines out of West Texas to the Agua Dulce Hub in South Texas and the Katy Hub — most recently, we looked at the record-busting plan by a WhiteWater Midstream-led consortium to build the 4.5-Bcf/d Solitude Pipeline, which will consist of twin 48-inch-diameter pipes from the Waha Hub to the Katy area.
The Natural Gas Master Class is a one-day online event focusing on understanding flow analysis, interpreting pipeline data and forecasting future flows. This course is designed to equip you with the knowledge and skills to effectively analyze the complexities of natural gas markets, flow analysis, and pipeline modeling. Join us online
October 21 | Online
But getting Permian gas to inland hubs like Katy and Agua Dulce — or to the Dallas/Fort Worth area, like Energy Transfer’s Hugh Brinson Pipeline — addresses only part of the challenge. The other part is, how do you get gas from there to where it’s demanded most, namely to LNG export terminals along the Gulf Coast between Port Arthur, TX, and Cameron Parish in the southwestern corner of Louisiana. Within that 40-mile stretch, about 59 MMtpa (~6.7 Bcf/d) of LNG export capacity is in operation and another 86 MMtpa (~9.4 Bcf/d) has reached a final investment decision (FID) and is either under construction or will be soon.
Sure, a sizable portion of that gas demand from existing and planned LNG export terminals will be met by the Haynesville Shale in northwestern Louisiana and northeastern Texas, but while Haynesville gas is produced at a relatively high cost, gas from the Permian is produced as a no-cost byproduct of crude oil-focused drilling and needs to find a home.
Midstream developers have been working hard the past couple of years to advance pipeline projects to transport more gas from the Katy area to Port Arthur and beyond. For example:
- A joint venture of WhiteWater Midstream and LNG exporter Venture Global is building the 3.5-Bcf/d Blackfin Pipeline (dashed purple line in Figure 1 below) from Colorado County, TX, (just west of Katy) to Jasper County, TX, near the Texas/Louisiana line. Blackfin is slated to start up in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027. It will connect in Jasper County with CP Express (dashed orange line), a 2.2-Bcf/d interstate line being built to supply feedgas to the CP2 LNG facility just across the border in Cameron Parish.
- Kinder Morgan is constructing the 2-Bcf/d Trident Pipeline (dashed dark-red line) from Katy to the Port Arthur area; it expects to finish Phase 1 (1.5 Bcf/d) in Q1 2027 and a 500-MMcf/d expansion (Phase 2) in Q4 2028.
- ARM Energy and PIMCO are jointly developing the 2.5-Bcf/d Mustang Express pipeline (dashed blue line), which by late 2029 or early 2030 will move gas from just west of Katy to the Port Arthur area.
About the song
“Don't Stop ’Til You Get Enough” was written by Michael Jackson and appears as the first song on side one of his debut studio solo album, Off the Wall. The disco-funk song is about searching for happiness and joy, and losing yourself in the music. It was the first solo song that Jackson wrote by himself. Released as the first single off the album in July 1979, it went to #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 Singles chart and has been certified 6X Platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). A music video for the song directed by Nick Saxton received heavy rotation on MTV. Personnel on the record were: Michael Jackson (vocals), Louis Johnson (bass), John Robinson (drums), Greg Phillinganes (keyboards), David Williams, Marlo Henderson (guitars), The Seawind Horns (horns), and Michael Jackson, Janet Jackson, Richard Heath, Paulinho de Costa and Sheila E. (percussion).
Off the Wall was recorded between December 1978 and June 1979 at Allen Zentz and Cherokee Studios in Hollywood and Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles; Quincy Jones was the producer. The album featured songwriting contributions from Jackson, Stevie Wonder, Paul McCartney, and David Foster. Released in August 1979, it went to #1 on the Billboard Top R&B Albums chart and #3 on the Billboard 200 Albums chart. It has been certified Diamond (10 million sales) by the RIAA. Five singles were released from the LP.
Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter and dancer, and one of the top-selling music artists of all time. He made his professional debut at the age of 6 as the lead singer of the Jackson 5. He rose to solo artist stardom with the release of his debut multi-platinum studio album, Off the Wall. As a solo artist, he released 10 studio albums, five soundtrack albums, 51 compilation albums and 67 singles and has sold over 500 million records worldwide. Jackson won 26 American Music Awards, four Brit Awards, 13 Grammy Awards, a Grammy Legend Award, and a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, and has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. He is a member of the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Songwriters Hall of Fame, Vocal Group Hall of Fame, and the Rhythm & Blues Music Hall of Fame. He starred in 11 films and documentaries. Jackson died at his home in Holmby Hills, CA, in June 2009 at 50.
